This study investigates multi-agent cooperation employing basic communication and computation capabilities. We develop an information exchange strategy allowing two agents to share information with each other, and prove that their shared information converges to the global mean under certain conditions. We demonstrate the efficacy of this information exchange strategy through simulated missions, including a search and rescue scenario, where agents successfully locate a target with limited computation and communication abilities. Additionally, the shared information enables agents to gain insight into their peers' processing and communication limitations, ultimately facilitating more accurate estimates of the target's location. We also explore an unsupervised learning approach, where agents autonomously develop a means of estimating the target's location without external guidance, and illustrate through simulations that shared information can expedite this learning process. Furthermore, we examine the effects of diverse communication and computation capabilities on collaborative outcomes, and find that even agents with vastly different capabilities can still benefit from shared information and collaborative learning. We validate our theoretical findings through extensive real-world experiments conducted over wireless networks. The outcomes of these experiments align with our theoretical predictions, showcasing the potential for effective collaborative outcomes even in scenarios involving dissimilar communication and computation capabilities. Moreover, the experimentally obtained data reveal that shared information can indeed facilitate learning and collaborative outcomes. Lastly, we observe that the dynamics of collaborative learning appear to exhibit characteristics of power-law behavior. Specifically, the distribution of iteration steps required by the agents to reach a predefined success threshold follows a power-law distribution. These findings underscore the inherent complexity and adaptability underlying collaborative systems, where components interact in a highly interconnected and dynamic manner. Moreover, this study provides a systematic approach for analyzing and modeling collaborative outcomes over simple forms of communication and computation, where local interactions give rise to intricate global patterns. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that collaborative systems can yield effective and predictable outcomes even under conditions of limited computation and communication, where components exhibit diverse behavior and iterative patterns. Moreover, the inherent complexity of these systems can be elucidated through transparent and predictive theoretical models. Lastly, these findings hold implications for the design of collaborative robotic systems, where agents possessing basic communication and computation capabilities can still benefit from shared information and collaborative learning. Cyber threats and attacks on computer systems and networks continue to escalate,
causing significant financial losses and compromising sensitive user data.
To address this issue, a new approach called Federated Learning (FL) is proposed
for developing a collaborative cyber threat intelligence exchange framework.
This innovative method enables the secure exchange and training of models on
distributed datasets from multiple entities, eliminating the need for central
collection and aggregation of data, thus maintaining data ownership and control.

The proposed framework consists of five distinct components:
1) data representation,
2) model development and distribution,
3) model aggregation,
4) security prototyping, and
5) protocol design.

A comprehensive case study is conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of FL in
unsupervised anomaly-based breach detection, using data from three distinct networks.
The results of these experiments demonstrate that FL-trained models can successfully
identify breaches in novel data with minimal data availability and optimal results. 

Furthermore, a prototype PPO-based security system is designed and tested to
secure FL operations against poisoning attacks, and a suitable protocol is proposed
for managing such attacks. The outcomes of these experiments indicate that FL can
be securely applied in real-world settings, providing a promising solution for
addressing data scarcity and training efficient breach detection systems. 

Ultimately, FL offers a promising solution for developing robust and efficient
cyber threat detection systems, overcoming the limitations of traditional monolithic
training methods and achieving promising results in anomaly-based breach detection. 

It is believed that FL will play a vital role in developing advanced and efficient
cybersecurity systems for detecting breaches and detecting cyber threats.

To overcome this limitation, we present a novel method called LimitedLabelPseudoTagging (LLPT) that leverages unlabeled graphs to create high-quality pseudo-labels for unseen graphs. This approach starts by assigning pseudo-labels to unlabeled graphs in an unsupervised manner, then uses them to enhance the model's performance on the unlabeled sets, ultimately updating the model with the best pseudo-labels through iterative optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that LLPT consistently improves the accuracy of GNNs on semi-supervised graph classification tasks across different datasets and settings, serving as a reliable unsupervised preprocessing technique for GNNs. The code for this method is available at https://github.com/erwanas/LLPT. Keywords: LimitedLabels, GNNs, Pseudo-Tagging, Semi-supervised, Graph Neural Networks. 

The proposed method has two key advantages:
1. It produces accurate pseudo-labels without relying on specific models, making it model-agnostic and easy to implement.
2. It iteratively improves the quality of pseudo-labels, incorporating the model's predictions and adapting to the available data.
These characteristics enable LLPT to effectively integrate unsupervised and supervised knowledge, resulting in consistent performance gains. 
While LLPT was specifically designed for graph classification tasks, its approach can be adapted to other settings, such as link prediction, node classification, and anomaly node detection. 
The method's success can be attributed to its ability to produce high-quality pseudo-labels, which serve as reliable labels for training GNN models on unlabeled graphs. 
By iteratively optimizing the pseudo-labels, LLPT effectively integrates the unsupervised and supervised knowledge, ultimately leading to improved performance.

Research on Jacobi elliptic functions originated in the early 19th century has a long history. Despite significant advancements in the field with the advent of computer technology, study of the elliptic modular functions themselves has remained limited due to the complexity of the Jacobi theta functions. However, the development of novel, high-efficiency algorithms in recent years has greatly enhanced the computational efficiency of Jacobi elliptic functions, thereby facilitating extensive research on the elliptic modular functions. This paper presents extensive findings on the computational models of Jacobi elliptic functions and their derivatives, along with mathematical expressions for their values, respectively. These results enable the computation of elliptic modular functions via the elliptic modular equation using the previously computed Jacobi elliptic functions. Consequently, the study of these functions has become significantly more accessible. Based on the computed data, we identified and confirmed previously undiscovered polynomial relationships among Jacobi elliptic functions, specifically the third-degree universal Airy polynomials. These polynomials provide valuable insights into the interactions among the Jacobi elliptic functions themselves, in addition to their previously established relationships with the Jacobi theta functions. Notably, these polynomials are degree-three polynomials in the variable $k^2$, where $k$ represents the modulus of the Jacobi elliptic functions. These universal Airy polynomials also exhibit a unique, highly regular pattern in their values and derivatives with respect to $k^2$. This pattern holds not only numerically but also analytically. This research not only expands our understanding of the elliptic modular functions themselves, but also opens up new avenues for studying the elliptic modular functions through the newly discovered universal Airy polynomials. Furthermore, these polynomials may also find practical applications in other fields due to their unique properties. Lastly, we verified that the third-degree universal Airy polynomials can seamlessly transition to the $k^2 \to 0$ limit, where they accurately model the hypergeometric functions in this specific context. These hypergeometric functions are fundamental building blocks in mathematics and appear extensively in mathematical calculations. This result not only validates the precision of the computed data at the $k^2 \to 0$ limit but also confirms the inherent, deep-seated connections among the Jacobi elliptic functions themselves, which were previously less apparent. This research has effectively illuminated these connections through the novel, degree-three universal Airy polynomials. These polynomials enable seamless computation of the elliptic modular functions even in extreme cases, such as $k^2 \to 0$

Precise smoke management in laparoscopic surgery is crucial to avoid damaging the operating room's equipment and the surgeon's vision. Current smoke detection methods rely on predefined thresholds in images, but this approach can be inefficient due to varying smoke properties. To develop a more effective smoke detection system, we propose a novel method that utilizes preprocessed images enriched with contextual information to accurately identify smoke. By applying image processing techniques, we aim to simplify the image data and increase its discriminative value for smoke identification. To achieve this, we employ pretraining on diverse surgical images and incorporate edge information, followed by a saliency map optimization framework to filter out irrelevant content. The performance of our image enhancement-based method was evaluated and demonstrated superior outcomes compared to standard threshold-based approaches. Additionally, we found that our image enhancement method can serve as a prefilter, further improving the smoke detection results. To validate the efficacy of our image enhancement method, we conducted comprehensive experiments on various datasets, analyzing the parameter dependence and inner connections between image enhancement and detection performance. Our study provides evidence that image enhancement techniques can be advantageous in preparing data for downstream analysis tasks, offering a new perspective on the role of image processing in medical image understanding. The proposed smoke detection framework, along with the optimized image enhancement method, can prevent equipment damage and ensure a clear vision for the surgeon in laparoscopic operations. Our research presents an adaptation of the conventional MOBILE gate strategy to withstand frequency fluctuations in an optical lattice trap. By analyzing the effects of laser cooling and trapped-ion interactions on the gate's performance, we developed a frequency-agility framework for implementing the MOBILE gate. This approach leverages the predictable frequency variations of multiple vibrational modes to create a stable frequency window for the gate, making it robust against frequency drifts and other disturbances. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method through numerical simulation, achieving an 85% MOBILE gate accuracy within a 100 kHz frequency uncertainty. Furthermore, our results indicate that increasing the number of motional modes can substantially enhance the gate's resilience to frequency fluctuations. This strategy provides a promising means of enhancing the MOBILE gate's performance in complex quantum algorithms, ultimately contributing to the development of frequency-resistant quantum computing with trapped ions. This work is part of a broader effort to address frequency-related challenges in quantum technology, as seen in a related study on the MOBILE gate's implementation using a 27-inch optical cavity. The Cotton tensor appears in gravity theories with an underlying flat structure, its appearance providing additional insights into the geometric and algebraic fundamentals of gravity. Furthermore, it acts as a conservative derivative, offering a more fundamental understanding of the law of conservation of gravity. In four-dimensional spacetime, the Cotton tensor is synonymous with the Weyl tensor, their equivalence derived from the Bianchi identities and the differential operators' consistent action across all differential forms. However, this equivalence does not extend to spacetimes of dimensions above four, where the Cotton tensor and Weyl tensor are distinct mathematical entities. Nonetheless, their relationship in four-dimensional spacetime sheds light on the Cotton tensor's meaning and significance in higher-dimensional spacetimes. In general, the Cotton tensor's appearance facilitates a more fundamental description of gravity, its relation to the Weyl tensor linking it to the geometric and algebraic fundamentals of general relativity and its conserved property making it a valuable tool in theoretical applications to gravity theories. This paper discusses these key properties of the Cotton tensor, its significance, and its applications to the foundations and testing of gravity theories. Additionally, it explores the Cotton tensor's appearance in second-order gravity theories, such as Poincaré and conformal gravity, establishing its generality in this class of theories and its potential as a foundational concept. Moreover, we derive and examine the Cotton tensor's expression in the de Sitter and anti-de Sitter spacetimes, its conserved property evident due to its relation to a divergence-like operator. This analysis reveals how the Cotton tensor's appearance and conserved property can be generalized to any spacetime structure, its applications extending to theories with non-zero cosmological constant. Finally, we investigate the Cotton tensor's appearance in Chern-Simons gravity, its relation to the Weyl tensor, and the conserved property derived from the Chern form of the Weyl tensor, uncovering a previously overlooked connection. This discussion clarifies that the Chern form of the Weyl tensor's appearance in Chern-Simons gravity, along with its conserved property, is a universal feature, its expressions determined solely by the spacetime structure and not by the specific charges incorporated into the theory. Consequently, this property enables us to express the charge action as a sum of a null action and a boundary term, the latter of which is a product of the Chern form of the spatial Cotton tensor and the Maxwell 2-form, thus simplifying the analysis of Chern-Simons gravity with gauge group SL(3,R) and revealing a previously overlooked

We introduce a concept of geometric duality for orthocomplemented lattices by combining ideas of direct products and Stone spaces with the categorical properties of joins and orthogonals. This leads to a demonstration of the duality between specific categories of orthocomplemented lattices and compact Hausdorff spaces equipped with two mappings defined by join and orthogonal operations. Furthermore, we establish a correspondence between upper continuous morphisms in the lattice category and continuous mappings between Stone spaces that preserve join and orthogonals. As a result, we can construct a Stone space whose lattice of closed subsets corresponds to a specific orthocomplemented sublattice of the lattice of closed subsets of a given compact Hausdorff space, and this Stone space is uniquely determined by the given sublattice through this geometric duality. Additionally, we show that geometric duality can be employed to demonstrate the categorical equivalence between lattices having a specific embedding property and compact Hausdorff spaces equipped with mappings preserving join and orthogonals. The concepts and techniques used here can be extended to more complex mathematical structures, such as systems with partial algebras, and these ideas can be utilized in diverse areas of mathematics. The proof of geometric duality can be visualized as a kind of topological mapping representation, and this concept can be related to the representation of lattices as topological spaces with mappings defined by join and orthogonals, as well as to the representation of commutative Banach lattices as spaces of linear operators with specific properties on certain types of lattices of bounded linear functionals. The ideas presented here can be seen as a form of spectral duality, and these duality theories share similarities with the algebraic duality theory developed by Malcev, Tarski, and others. The geometric duality theory introduced here can be utilized to construct new concrete representations of a wide range of lattices within the framework of Stone spaces, and this can be seen as a generalization of the classical Stone representation theorem. Furthermore, geometric duality can be employed to study upper continuous morphisms between lattices with specific embedding properties, and this can be related to the study of continuous mappings between compact Hausdorff spaces that preserve join and orthogonals. We introduce a visual representation system that translates Coq proof scripts into tabular forms, which can be exported as $\LaTeX$ or PDF files. Our tool aims to facilitate learning and proof review by providing an interactive visual representation of each step in a proof. Consequently, this system enables educators and reviewers to utilize the proofs without relying on the Coq program, thereby allowing them to be printed or shared in other forms, as opposed to the more conventional hypertext or markdown formats. Moreover, as the visual representation is generated from the proof, it inherits all properties of the original, including soundness. Our case studies demonstrate that even highly complex proofs with numerous macros can be visualized effectively within a few milliseconds. Furthermore, this system is adaptable and can be utilized with custom visualizations of various types. We have visualized over 50 proofs of notable facts in mathematics, which can be found on our dedicated website for easy access. These visualizations not only enhance the understanding of each mathematical object but also make the proofs more accessible and easier to comprehend. Our system is compatible with the latest versions of Coq and can be installed using the OPAM package manager under the name coq-psv. As an added feature, we have also integrated a 3D visualisation option, which can be used to generate interactive 3D visual representations of proofs for educational purposes, as demonstrated in our study on the geometric interpretation of Lafont, Bedarida and Cohen's Calcul du Quotient Truncation. This 3D visualisation integrates concepts of group theory and the quotient group, rendering the proof in a visually appealing 3D structure that facilitates comprehension and learning. In interior point methods (IPMs), an iterative solution formulation is often employed to tackle large-scale linear systems that arise when moving within the interior of a constrained optimization problem. This article examines the convergence of iterative methods such as the Conjugate Gradient and Minimum Residual algorithms in the context of IPMs. We propose and evaluate an original termination criterion that can be applied when premultiplying the system by a direction of optimal descent (DOD). This new criterion enables the precise identification of when an optimal or near-optimal solution is achieved without resorting to additional approximations or the explicit computation of residual norms in subproblems. This approach is particularly beneficial within the context of IPMs, where such information is already readily available due to the primal-dual interior point algorithm (PDIPA) that is used. Therefore, the proposed criterion can be easily integrated into Krylov solvers without requiring further modifications. To substantiate the efficacy of this criterion, extensive numerical experiments are conducted across a diverse set of problem instances, encompassing sparse finite element and finite difference linear systems, as well as structured matrices stemming from quadratic optimization problems and the stochastic blocking crossroads traffic routing problem. These numerical tests demonstrate that utilizing the proposed criterion results in fewer iterations and faster overall solution times compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, the code used in these experiments has been openly contributed under the permissive APACHE 2.0 license. It is now freely accessible at the following repository: https://github.com/JuliaOpt.KristofIPM/blob/master/contrib/InteriorPointMethods/inside\_PDIIPA/inside\_PDIIPA.jl. This includes a detailed documentation of the code at the following link: https://juliaopt.github.io/InteriorPointMethods/html/inside\_PDIIPA.html#InteriorPointMethods.inside\_PDIIPA.inside\_PDIIPA.

These incidents are often isolated and discussed in isolation, lacking a broader context. While the precision may not significantly impact low-order approximations in our example, it could substantially influence higher-order outcomes and may even necessitate all-order summation. This method, though informal, can provide insights into the feasibility of solving the RG puzzle. Assembling a complete and error-free genome from short, overlapping reads has become more manageable with long-read sequencing technologies. A popular approach, de novo assembly using chromosomal scaffolds, typically requires creating large, continuous strings of bases. In memory-constrained systems, compressing base sequences by converting them into paths in a de Bruijn graph has become a standard solution. However, this compression method inevitably introduces artificial edges and nodes, necessitating decompression and thus limiting the size of the genomes that can be efficiently handled. To address this issue, we have developed a new, parallel algorithm that creates contiguous, compressed sequences directly from the compressed graph, bypassing the need for base-level memory. By efficiently using multiple processors and memory modules, our approach can assemble larger, higher-quality chromosomal scaffolds than existing methods. Our results show that the technique not only outperforms current state-of-the-art de novo assembly pipelines but also extends the limits of what is achievable in terms of genome size and chromosome number. With the rise of long-read sequencing, this innovation will revolutionize the field of genomics by making it possible to sequence complex, large-genome organisms. Furthermore, the technique has far-reaching potential applications across a broad spectrum of biological research and medicine. This approach offers enhanced precision and a broader applicability, expanding the scope for mass measurements in nuclear and particle physics, particularly for particles with lower natural isochronous properties. The research outcomes from the HIRAU ring serve as a benchmark for similar facilities worldwide, including the CSNS HIA beam facility, which will be utilized in future experiments to measure the masses of additional nuclei. The exceptional capabilities of $B\rho$-defined isochronous mass spectrometry will significantly contribute to the development of a global least-squares fit in the QCD matter at finite baryon density and various nuclear physics theories for quark and nucleus phase transitions. The team will also investigate the mass of the $^{46}K$ nucleus and evaluate the feasibility of using $B\rho$-defined isochronous mass spectrometry for precise mass measurements of the $^{42}S$ and $^{42}K$ nuclei, which exhibit lower natural isochronous properties. Research has shown that procedural oversight in intelligent systems is highly desired, with studies demonstrating how these systems can learn to make predictions about their actions in various domains including medicine, commerce, and education. To advance this area of study, we conducted a comprehensive review of a specific type of predictive procedural oversight called "prescriptive procedure monitoring", which involves using predictive models to guide system interaction and has significant applications in its own right. This type of oversight differs from the more traditional "procedural monitoring", which focuses solely on tracking and correcting actual system processes. With prescriptive procedure monitoring, users can express their preferences for desired system behaviors, and intelligent systems can generate and predict alternative procedures to achieve those preferences. To explore this area further, we developed a framework that incorporates various key considerations and applied it to a real-world scenario related to online commerce. Our results from an online experiment with 180 participants revealed that users value predictive procedural oversight and can benefit from it, even when the underlying procedures remain hidden. Our findings also showed that "abandon-procedure" - a predicted system behavior that aligns with user preferences - is a significant predictor of user satisfaction. Our work provides a foundation for future research into the effective implementation and evaluation of prescriptive procedural oversight in intelligent systems. At the same time, our study also raises important research questions and suggests potential avenues for further exploration, as evidenced by the comments and additional ideas shared by the participants in the online experiment. These comments also highlight an intriguing paradox - while users value predictive procedural oversight, they may also prefer the original system behavior if it leads to better outcomes, underscoring the importance of "in the wild" testing of these predictive models and the need for more systematic research on the underlying user system dynamics. Furthermore, our study also suggests that predictive models could be improved by incorporating user-generated content and that the effectiveness of the "show-procedure" strategy could be influenced by system-generated explanations that are tailored to user preferences. Finally, our results also indicate that the effectiveness of the "abandon-procedure" strategy could be influenced by the level of user expertise and that the implementation of predictive procedural oversight could be affected by factors such as system transparency and user expectations. These additional findings are presented in a set of research questions and potential avenues for future research. To facilitate this, we make our code, data, and experiment design publicly available. In various social phenomena, individuals tend to adopt certain perspectives or views that are influenced by the perspectives of those around them. At the same time, these individuals also hold their own perspectives or structural views on how others in the group will behave. We examine the interaction of these two concepts, developing a framework that combines both and is referred to as the'structural equilibrium perspective dynamic.' Through an in-depth analysis, we find that this dynamic converges to a state of social equilibrium where every individual has the same perspective. Prior to this convergence, however, we identify a preliminary state where nearly everyone shares a widely adopted'main view,' while a smaller group of individuals holds distinct, minority perspectives. We have found that this preliminary state provides a level of assurance that is limited in nature, as it does not guarantee the absence of all social uncertainty. Nevertheless, it does provide a level of certainty or assurance, which can be quantified. We have also found that the likelihood of this limited assurance occurring is not solely dependent on the initial distribution of structural views but also on how those views are distributed among individuals who adopt the main view and those who hold distinct, minority perspectives. We have established a method for calculating the probability of this limited assurance, which can be thought of as providing 'limited social assurance.' We use this concept in an exploration of a fundamental question: what is the likelihood that social interactions will provide some level of certainty or assurance in a group setting? We have derived formulas and provided numerical results for this inquiry in various social equilibrium states, as well as in both large and small group settings. Ultimately, we have found that while structural views are highly uncertain in the short term, as individuals continuously update their perspectives based on the actions of those around them, a state of social equilibrium where every individual has the same perspective leads to a level of certainty or assurance, as well as a more stable and less uncertain environment. We introduce a new, compact representation of a function, $f$, tailored to take advantage of its variable importance, without requiring a specific ordering. This representation, called the BPD, enables efficient computation of a function's minimum proximal residual and its gradient, particularly for complex models with a large number of variables. This algorithm is capable of solving challenging inference problems in models that typically pose difficulties for machine learning and optimization. In multi-modal distribution fusion, combining data from different sources to localise objects, the timing of signals can vary greatly. This paper presents a new asynchronous audio-visual fusion approach for localising objects in 3D space. The approach is tested in a practical scenario where a robot searches for items hidden in a room, processing visual data while receiving audio cues from its speaker. The method's efficacy is confirmed through experiments conducted in simulated and real-world environments, the latter being a hospital simulation to raise safety considerations. The findings indicate that the proposed method localises objects more accurately than those using synchronous fusion and single-modal approaches. The code is openly accessible on GitHub. A well-known phenomenon, the "desert" in exoplanetary mass distribution, lacks Earth-mass and Neptune-mass planets orbiting close to stars in certain regions of their mass and orbital radius.  This phenomenon, specifically in close orbit planets (less than 4 days), has been extensively studied using various datasets.  This study investigated whether a "desert" in sub-Saturn mass planets (saturn mass minus half that of Jupiter) existing in close orbit (less than 4 days) around stars in the CORALIE/HARPS radial velocity sample.  By comparing observed detected planets to a set of mock planets, this study found no evidence to support the presence of a "desert" in sub-Saturn mass planets.  95% confidence interval indicated that the ratio of detected to mock planets for planets with a mass between 10 and 100 times that of Earth, and an orbital radius between 0.04 and 4 astronomical units, is greater than 0.01.  By further analysis, this study found that the non-detection of a "desert" could be due to migration of planets from the outer planetary disk, a phenomenon also supported by other studies.  This research also suggested possible limitations of the radial velocity detection method in explaining the "desert" phenomenon.  Further investigation is needed to resolve the discrepancies between the mock and detected planet ratios.  This discrepancy could provide valuable insight into how planetary mass and orbit are created and destroyed in planetary systems.  This research did find evidence to support the planetary mass and orbit generation model that migrates planets from the outer planetary disk.  This model also showed that the primary destruction of close-orbit planets likely occurs due to planetary instability.  As a result, this study found that the number of planets in the sample that could have been destroyed due to instability is greater than the "desert" gap ratio, and the destruction of planets in planetary instability events likely fills the "desert" gap in the planetary mass and orbit distribution in the CORALIE/HARPS sample.  This research found similar results when using a different set of mock planets that were also consistent with the exoplanetary mass and orbit distribution in the Kepler catalog.  This study also found that planetary instability is the most plausible explanation for the "desert" phenomenon, and further study is needed to compare the radial velocity detectability of planets resulting from planetary instability and migration from the outer planetary disk. The ability of Dark Matter (DM) to pass undetected makes it an ideal candidate for its particles being weakly interacting and having very low mass, which could result in the emission of only gamma rays from astrophysical sources, experimenters being able to search for DM in labs using highly sensitive instruments, and the formation of only small, dense structures in the universe with the loss of energy during Big Bang Nucleosynthesis, which is not accounted for by the Standard Model. A model that fits this description is the Leptophobic model, which modifies the Standard Model's particle interactions in a specific way, resulting in DM being invisible to electromagnetic observation but releasing energy in the form of gamma rays when annihilating. However, the model's particle interactions are further restricted, which makes it difficult to create a compressed DM scenario where the energy released from DM annihilation does not exceed the gamma-ray observations' limits. The Compressed DM scenario is only possible if a certain type of heavy particles are present in the universe in large numbers, which is difficult to reconcile with astrophysical data. The alignment of supermassive black holes in galaxies has been extensively studied, with contradictory results, although consensus is building that edge-on galaxies have a higher alignment.  To resolve these discrepancies, we investigated the alignment of different types of active galaxies, considering various host galaxy properties.  Employing a large sample of 1069 active galaxies from the SDSS, we analyzed the orientation of major axes in relation to north.  Focusing on a subset of 383 star-forming active galaxies, we found that the major axes of radio-emitting galaxies are aligned at an angle of approximately 44 degrees with respect to north, especially in edge-on galaxies.  In contrast, the alignments of non-radio galaxies and other types, such as broad-line galaxies, show significantly larger angles, ranging from 49 to 63 degrees.  Furthermore, we discovered that the alignments of active galaxies in edge-on galaxies vary by type, ranging from 41 to 53 degrees.  Using simulated data, we verified that variations in alignment by type are statistically significant.  Moreover, we found that the alignments of active galaxies depend on their host galaxy types, with notable differences depending on the galaxy type.  These findings imply that the growth mechanisms of different active galaxies may be distinct, with possible implications for their black hole alignment and potential observable effects on galaxy formation.  Consequently, investigating the relationships between various active galaxies and their host galaxies is essential to understanding the planet's alignment phenomenon, particularly its connection to supermassive black holes.  Based on our data, we propose that the alignments of active galaxies are influenced by their host galaxies, leading to distinct galaxy distributions in different orientations.  Interestingly, we discovered that the alignments of active galaxies are not random but are correlated with host galaxy types, with notable differences depending on whether galaxies are star-forming or passive and, specifically, whether they emit radio signals.  These findings provide new insights into the relationships between various active galaxies and their host galaxies, ultimately shedding light on the large-scale alignment phenomenon in our galaxy universe.  To summarize our findings, we observed that the alignments of active galaxies depend on their type and host galaxy properties, leading to distinct distributions in different orientations.  Consequently, investigating the relationships between various active galaxies and their host galaxies is essential to understanding the planet's alignment phenomenon and the growth mechanisms of supermassive black holes.  To further study this, we plan to analyze simulated data to verify that the alignments of active galaxies vary by type and to delves deeper into the distinct distributions in different orientations.

This repository will be developed to provide up-to-date climate information and enable the development of location and season-specific engagement strategies. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we constructed a climate information repository for the Gulf Coast region in the United States and used it to create engaging climate change communication campaigns for Houston and New Orleans during the fall and spring seasons, respectively. Our methods successfully yielded high-quality, customizable climate information that resulted in positive responses from community members. This approach can be replicated and adapted for various regions and initiatives. Additionally, the climate information repository can be further utilized to address other environmental concerns, such as storm management and environmental justice. It has the potential to be a powerful tool for community-based climate communication and engagement projects. By leveraging pseudo-labels on an unseen domain, our proposed model's extraction accuracy can be enhanced. Experimental results demonstrate that our model surpasses a control model in extraction accuracy, particularly when applied to more diverse domains. Our research highlights the challenges of recruiting volunteers for scientific computations by demonstrating how simple it is to deceive users with fake tasks that mimic real computations. We developed Pando, a platform that enables remote execution of computations on users' devices without requiring direct access to their resources. This is achieved by relying on users' browsers to transmit computational results, thereby preserving network privacy and security. A major innovation of Pando is its ability to verify the integrity of computed data using signature chains, even in the event of connection disruptions or malicious activities. A collaborative trial involving over 10,000 participants from diverse educational backgrounds showed that Pando's efficient balancing of computational load and response time can be further improved by dynamically adjusting the level of computational detail based on users' device capabilities. This was accomplished through an analysis of users' browser versions and a novel assessment of their devices' processing capabilities, which we refer to as the'slowness factor'. This concept is particularly useful in projects that involve analyzing large datasets and require human involvement to generate specific results, as to do so, researchers would need to develop bespoke algorithms or integrate existing software with complex technical frameworks. In contrast, Pando's user-centric approach allows researchers to focus on core scientific problems while leveraging the computational power of distributed resources, all without compromising security and data integrity. Further information can be found on our website at https://pando.webc.hu/. To prevent their use, a secure learning framework is needed to train these algorithms securely. Currently available approaches either rely on insecure garbled circuits or disregard data privacy, which is not acceptable. To address this gap, we present an innovative solution, named Flatee, that enables collaborative training across multiple parties, while maintaining confidentiality, based on the principles of Trusted Execution Environments and Secure Multi-Party Computation. This approach allows multiple parties to jointly develop a model without exposing their datasets, by which, a secure neural network is constructed, and the parameters are jointly optimized, without any data exchange. To evaluate its effectiveness, we implemented Flatee using TensorFlow and PyTecHE, under realistic scenarios, wherein two to three parties collaborated to achieve comparable results, outperforming the existing state-of-the-art approaches, notably, Federated Learning, by at least 71% in terms of communication overhead. Moreover, our approach demonstrates robust resilience against adversarial attacks and efficient computation outside the vulnerable cloud environments. This groundbreaking work presents the first known collaboration among multiple parties, using Trusted Execution Enclaves, to train machine learning models securely. This paper introduces timeloops, a PoC-based method for automatically generating system call filters for containerized microservices based on their behavior. The primary challenge in developing system call filters lies in accurately pinpointing the service functions that generate output that requires access to sensitive resources. A comprehensive understanding of a service's dynamics is necessary to create reliable system call filters, as misidentified functions may lead to denial-of-service attacks or unauthorized access vulnerabilities. The extraction and pinning process for a service function can be labor-intensive, prompting the development of timeloops, an automated tool for generating system call filters from service functions.

The main concept underlying timeloops is the transient state of a service, which is characterized by short-term interactions among functions. The framework employs a technique called transient analysis to identify the set of functions that correspond to a service's temporary state. By applying this approach, timeloops determines the set of functions for a service, eliminating the need for human intervention to verify function sequences. The framework also incorporates an algorithm to generate system call filters based on a service's transient state, using negative samples to fine-tune the filters and ensure they accurately reflect the service behavior. Experimental results demonstrate that timeloops produces effective system call filters for various benchmarks with minimal false positives. The framework serves as a PoC for automated system call filtering and can be adapted to other programming languages with minimal modifications. The adaptation involves replacing the compiler-based code signing used in our implementation, which we discuss in the conclusion. The experimental outcomes validate the suitability of timeloops as a system call filter tool. The code for timeloops is publicly available on GitHub at the specified link. Recent studies at the Galactica Center near the Milky Way's center have discovered anisotropic velocity distributions of young stars at varying distances from the galaxy's center.  This finding has been linked to their stellar orbits around a supermassive black hole as studied in the stable segregation theory.  We applied this theoretical model to multiple supermassive black holes within our own galaxy and eight neighboring galaxies to understand the relationship between their velocity anisotropy and distance from the black hole.  The theoretical model supported previous findings that the anisotropy of young stars in the Milky Way is consistent with the stable segregation theory.  Furthermore, our research revealed that the anisotropy of other galaxies does not support the stable segregation theory, though our results may be influenced by limited data availability.  We have developed a new method to quantify the level of segregation in a galaxy and used it to determine the segregation level for our nearest galaxies, which suggests minimal segregation in these galaxies.  This research was conducted using the general relativity framework and confirms that our findings are independent of the method used to model galactic velocity distributions.  These breakthroughs provide new avenues for studying the central structure of galaxies and the behavior of matter surrounding supermassive black holes. Additionally, we found that a specific characteristic of the segregation theory known as $\beta_{\rm ss}$ varies in an unpredictable manner, defying earlier expectations and instead behaving in a chaotic and dynamic manner, and we found that a previous assumption that the radial velocity dispersion of stars close to a black hole should be higher than further away is not necessarily true in all cases and should not be made without considering the effects of the black hole. Finally, we found that a particular distance at which the velocity anisotropy of stars in the Milky Way changes sign does not match our calculations using the stable segregation theory. We introduce a basic model predictive regulation (MPR) framework that integrates random disturbances into control systems. In this context, MPR functions as a sequential, online optimization method, generating control inputs in a short-term, open-loop manner to manage random system disruptions. By iteratively using recent system data to update the optimization model, the algorithm adapts to unexpected disturbances, ultimately converging towards a stable equilibrium. Through numerical analysis and graphical visualization, we examine how changes in the size of optimization problems affect the algorithm's performance, observing how adjustments in the finite horizon model size influence the final equilibrium point and demonstrating the trade-offs inherent in tuning these parameters. Furthermore, under specific structural assumptions regarding the disturbance term, we prove that the algorithm attains a globally asymptotic convergence property known as almost global convergence, indicating that the sequence of computed open-loop controls eventually converges to a stable closed-loop strategy. The implementation details and theoretical findings outlined here can serve as a prototypical approach for addressing a broad class of control problems involving complex nonlinear systems subject to arbitrary disturbances. Furthermore, the observed behavior provides valuable insights into the computational challenges and theoretical limitations of using MPR as a control strategy. The associated code for reproducing the results in this study is publicly accessible at https://github.com/CPJockey/rmpc_code. Additionally, a detailed tutorial on the underlying algorithms can be found at https://github.com/CPJockey/rmpc_tutorial. The mathematical framework and algorithmic developments presented here can be applied to a wide range of control applications, including but not limited to: power systems, as examined in the simulation example; transportation systems; and industrial processes. Creating advanced artificial intelligence systems has proven challenging due to the inherent power consumption efficiency of brain-inspired approaches, which often require low voltage levels. To overcome this limitation, researchers need simulators that can test algorithms before implementing them on specialized neuroprocessor chips. To address this issue, a team developed Brian2Loihi, a simulator package that emulates the behavior of neural networks on the Loihi chip using the Brian simulator. Brian2Loihi was utilized to verify the reliability of neural network algorithms, which were later successfully implemented on the chip. Furthermore, the team enhanced Brian2Loihi with energy consumption estimation capabilities to evaluate the efficiency of these algorithms. By comparing numerical solutions, the team validated the accuracy of Brian2Loihi and found it to be compatible with the native Loihi simulator, with Brian2Loihi offering additional features and greater flexibility in network designs. Additionally, Brian2Loihi's energy consumption estimates closely matched the results of actual measurements on the Loihi chip. By integrating Brian2Loihi into the design cycle of neuroprocessor chips, researchers can optimize and refine brain-inspired AI algorithms to run efficiently on such chips. The team made Brian2Loihi open-source to facilitate the inclusion of simulators in the neural network design process. A comprehensive tutorial is available for those interested in using Brian2Loihi to design and train neural networks on conventional computers, which can later be implemented on the Loihi chip or similar neuroprocessor chips. The source code is accessible on GitHub at: https://github.com/spinnler/brian2loihi. The project website provides further documentation and information at: https://brian2loihi.readthedocs.io. The team welcomes contributions and suggestions for improving Brian2Loihi and its utility in neural network design. Estimates of energy consumption can be accessed through the project website at: https://brian2loihi.github.io/energy-estimator. The universal approximation principle states that a feedforward neural network with a single hidden layer can accurately approximate any continuous function with a finite input space. However, implementing this concept practically proves difficult due to the lack of a clear method to determine the required number of hidden layer neurons. Prior research proposed relying on trial and error or stopping criteria based on convergence metrics, but these approaches often lead to suboptimal results. This study introduces a novel method to determine the ideal network architecture by directly estimating the number of hidden layer neurons needed, thereby eliminating the need for iterative trial and error. Our approach is gradient-free, computationally efficient, and generalizable to various neural network configurations, outperforming existing methods in function fitting and machine learning applications. Furthermore, we showcase the suitability of our method for real-world regression problems. The proposed algorithm is also available on GitHub under the name 'UniversalApproximator'. In this research, the quarkonium disintegration characteristics in a non-zero momentum anisotropy and finite baryonic potential are investigated within the N-dimensional space. An advanced mathematical model is developed to examine the quarkonium disintegration behavior in both pure gluonic and quark-gluon plasma environments. By utilizing quasi-particle methods and considering finite baryonic potential, the Debye mass is determined in a simplified manner. This model is then employed to analyze the quarkonium disintegration as a function of temperature, momentum anisotropy, and baryonic potential. Additionally, the baryonic potential dependence of the Debye mass and its impact on quarkonium disintegration are thoroughly discussed. This theory is further compared with existing quarkonium disintegration characteristics models, such as the hard thermal loop (HTL) theory. Furthermore, the implications of non-zero momentum anisotropy and baryonic potential on quarkonium disintegration are explored. This research provides novel insights into quarkonium disintegration behavior in a heated, baryon-rich QCD environment. Specifically, the baryonic potential is found to enhance the quarkonium disintegration rate at low temperatures. This effect is more pronounced in the presence of momentum anisotropy. Moreover, the research reveals that the Debye mass is sensitive to baryonic potential, especially at low temperatures. However, the theoretical framework of learning in complex-valued neural networks remains poorly understood, hindering its practical implementation. To enhance a VM's security, the communication between the VM and the host should be limited to necessary protocols only.  Typically, a VM uses a standard network library for communication, which often includes various tools such as network drivers and transport layers.  A network library typically includes several components such as transport layers, file transfer mechanisms, and connection management.  When a VM makes a function call to interact with the host's system, it uses the framework to send a request to the host, which is received as an interrupt by the host's CPU. The response is then written to the requestor's device or file system as an I/O operation, and the process may repeat until the requested operation is complete. The research also finds that the host's network traffic is not hidden from the VM's network, and the study confirms that the framework does not encrypt the data exchange. A sender attempts to transmit a value of x to a receiver through a channel while an adversary may also interfere with an unknown value of y. The receiver uses an estimator and is required to guarantee that the probability of a large error does not exceed a specified limit. In early 2020, as the COVID-19 pandemic spread across China, the government launched a nationwide health education initiative to counteract the spread of digital misinformation. Our research focuses on the outcome of this effort. By analyzing popular rumors in China prior to the pandemic and during its peak, our findings show that these digital misconceptions largely mirrored existing social and political concerns pre-dating the outbreak. Conversely, the pandemic gave rise to new rumors largely devoid of political undertones, instead focusing on everyday issues arising from the crisis. Our research quantifies the effectiveness of the government's efforts, revealing that targeted counter-narratives can significantly mitigate the dissemination of digital misinformation. However, once a rumor gains traction, our models show that dissemination campaigns have diminished impact. These findings offer valuable insights into digital rumor dissemination in China and provide analytical metrics to gauge the country's digital health education initiatives. Additionally, they contribute to broader knowledge regarding digital misinformation spread and offer practical suggestions to control rumor dissemination more effectively. Dimensionality reduction techniques are widely employed in hyperspectral image analysis to enhance processing efficiency. The Spectral Dimensionality Minimization method (SDM) is one such approach, reducing spectral data dimensions while minimizing reconstruction error. While effective in general image analysis, its impact on hyperspectral image classification is not well understood. In this study, we investigate the effects of SDM on hyperspectral pixel classification capabilities. By applying SDM to a dataset comprising synthetic images, we observe that spectral dimensions are reduced, and reconstruction error increases with SDM parameters. However, this dimensionality reduction hinders hyperspectral pixel classification performance in these synthetic datasets. To confirm these findings, we evaluate and replicate these results using real-world hyperspectral images, demonstrating that spectral dimensions reduced by SDM can compromise hyperspectral pixel classification in natural scenes. Despite the presence of multiple NLP frameworks, a common misconception is that a single framework, e.g. type theory, is essential for natural language semantics.  In contrast, we demonstrate that any natural language semantics framework can be reduced to a straightforward functional representation.  Furthermore, we show that similar reduction possibilities exist for models focusing on distributional semantics, semantics-based machine learning, and generative frameworks. Such an approach enables a more unified understanding of NLP problems, allowing for cross-fertilization and collaborative work across different NLP disciplines.  In particular, we outline the reduction of Montague's intensional type theory in eight steps and type theory in six steps. However, quantum physics-based models can describe the behavior of hydrogen bonds in proteins and predict the displacement of amide protons. This study proposes a new approach that integrates such predictions with protein structures. We evaluated this method on a set of high-resolution protein crystal structures and found that it effectively identifies residues with abnormal hydrogen bonding or other distortions in protein structures. Specifically, the model pinpointed 12% of residues in proteins as problematic based on a threshold of 170 cm^-1 difference in predicted and observed frequencies. Notably, nearly all proteins studied had at least 5 residues that matched this criterion. When applied to proteins with known issues, the model successfully flagged 90% of residues in problem-protein complexes and 82% of residues in proteins with proposed flaws. Furthermore, the model accurately predicted abnormal properties for residues involved in protein interactions, including those playing a crucial role in the function and stability of proteins. Finally, the model was used to improve protein structures by adjusting the positions of carbon atoms in proteins. By using the model, we were able to correct distorted regions in proteins and found that the overall root mean square deviation (RMSD) decreased by 0.08 angstroms in all proteins studied and as much as 1.20 angstroms in some problem-protein complexes. In typical educational settings, the goal is for the teacher to provide valuable insights to their students, educating and guiding them in the process.  We propose an alternative model, where we consider the teacher as part of a two-player game, where the teacher competes against the level of student understanding.  Our "minimax" approach aims for the optimal strategy for the teacher to choose the most effective methods to reach their desired educational objectives, given the knowledge of what works best, which we refer to as the "optimal control set".  We apply this concept in the context of online forums, where we simulate a teacher seeking to disseminate a new idea to users, and a "student" resisting this idea, with the current state representing user feedback and comments.  Our goal is for the teacher to ultimately achieve their goal and reach a state of "knowledge acceptance", while the resistant user may employ various strategies of obstruction, including dispersal, distraction, and obstruction.  The maximin approach gives the teacher the strategy to maximize the minimum level of educational progress achieved, which translates to finding the optimal policy to achieve their desired outcome.  We use reinforcement learning to find this optimal policy, and in our experiments, the simulated teacher successfully achieved their goal despite initial resistance from the users.  This model can be applied in a variety of educational settings, where the teacher must compete against the level of student understanding, such as in the context of online education. In this study, we examine the temporal development of a complexity metric, specifically the normalized entropy of melody similarity matrices, applied to a substantial dataset of 250,000 songs from four decades of the 20th and 21st centuries. Our results show that the average melody complexity of this dataset increases over time, with a significant shift towards higher complexity in the 2010s compared to earlier decades. Additionally, sub-analysis of song sections and instruments reveals a parallel increase in complexity for all components, and reveals that the leading cause of this complexity growth is the expansion of musical vocabulary rather than increased dissonance. Our work has practical applications in music generation, where developers can now create more realistic and naturally evolving melodies using either evolutionary algorithms or Markov chain-based methods. Furthermore, our findings contribute to the broader field of musical informatics, providing quantitative insights into the gradual modernization of musical data. All code and dataset used in this study have been made publicly available. Additionally, we have developed a interactive visualization tool that demonstrates the relationship between musical complexity and time. While this method is widely accepted, working with the process parameters in a model based on a Poisson distribution can be complicated. In order to simplify the analysis, we propose a new technique that reduces the number of difficult-to-handle parameters by substituting them with others that are more easily estimated. These substitute parameters have a direct relationship with the parameters we initially worked with, and are more suitable for statistical inference. We then develop a method of statistical inference for these new parameters, based on a specific type of consistent estimators known as Bayesian quantile estimators, which are particularly useful in the case where data is limited. This method of inference is further tested in simulations and in an actual study, where the focus is on understanding the characteristics of rare events such as strong earthquakes and extreme floods. The proposed approach demonstrates improved performance and greater accuracy when compared to other established methods. We also provide a detailed explanation of the theoretical underpinnings of this method, which is based on extreme value theory. In the context of Offline Reinforcement Learning, we investigate robustness to data corruption. The problem is framed as selecting the most resilient policy when a certain percentage of the data is artificially manipulated. Building on prior research on optimal transport, we develop a framework for data corruption resistance and propose a new metric. The theoretical foundations of this concept are established by proving convergence of empirical correlations to true correlations. The results are supported by experimental studies, which demonstrate that our approach outperforms comparison methods under various corruption scenarios. The code used in these experiments can be accessed at https://github.com/epfl-iclr-2022/corrupted_olforl. Further details are available in the supplementary materials, with additional results and tools in the appendix.

This research addresses the issue of optimal control for a one-dimensional heat equation, which initially involves a state variable subject to time-varying and temperature-dependent boundary controls. A real control $u=u(t,x)$ is considered to be able to modify the heat conductivity on the right boundary of the domain, while the left boundary remains non-controllable. A cost function is introduced to measure the cost of this control, which promotes a rapid transition from a given initial state to a target state. To resolve this optimal control problem, which is ill-posed due to its non-differentiable coefficients, a regularization method is employed. It involves replacing the original cost function with a family of smoother objectives. However, the conventional approach requires the boundary control to be constant, which limits the system's ability to adjust the heat conductivity. Consequently, additional terms are introduced to model an abrupt change in the heat conductivity, called impulsive manageability. It allows for sudden changes in the heat conductivity on small intervals, which are compensated by adjusting the heat conductivity on adjacent impulsive intervals. To resolve the related non-differentiable terms, a logarithmic transformation is applied to the cost function, which makes the optimization problem more amenable to analysis. Using a logarithmic transformation, a logarithmic curvature is defined and used to establish the optimality conditions for a family of optimized boundary controls. To achieve reliable performance in real-world applications, models of text must function accurately both in- and out-of-distribution. However, current models often fail to identify their limitations when encountering unfamiliar data sources, such as newly emerging domains or languages. In this research, we provide an in-depth analysis of out-of-distribution text categories and propose a straightforward approach to identify them. Our approach relies on testing how text representations handle text transformations that mimic shifts in language characteristics, and we provide comprehensive evaluations on a diverse range of datasets that encompass a wide spectrum of out-of-distribution text categories, including domain-specific, domain-crossing, style variations, and foreign languages. Our proposed methodology enables the detection of out-of-distribution text domains with high accuracy and provides valuable insights into the out-of-distribution text categories encountered in the evaluated datasets. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method can improve the performance of models by selectively discarding out-of-distribution examples in training and bypassing irrelevant tasks at inference. Our approach offers a flexible framework for out-of-distribution text identification and can be adapted to accommodate various requirements in practical applications. The proposed method, along with a comprehensive set of out-of-distribution text categories called ODIE, is made available to support the development of reliable text models that can effectively handle unfamiliar data sources. Utilizing quantum-thermal fluctuations, molecular motors can draw in energy to generate mechanical work at the molecular level. One theory is that work is produced within a Brownian dynamical framework by utilizing fluctuating potentials. However, these models rely on the assumption of thermal equilibrium, which isn't necessarily the case when engines are fueled by inelastic electron tunneling. We've developed a new approach that views the engine as a quantum system undergoing rapid decay, with its environment modeled as a collection of fluctuating electronic states. We've found that this setup allows the engine to transition between two states with varying tunneling rates, effectively harnessing the difference in rates to perform mechanical work in the slow decay regime. In this regime, we've developed a method for calculating the engine's irreversibility and demonstrated that it can function as a thermal machine, even in the absence of an explicit temperature definition, by utilizing the concept of entropy production based on the environment's electronic distribution. We've verified the validity of our approach through numerical simulations in both one and two dimensions. Additionally, we've explored the generalization of our model to accommodate multiple states and found that the engine can operate in a bistable regime, powered by a difference in rates for each state, which also allows it to maintain a non-zero current even when all rates are equalized. We've further extended our model to account for variations in tunneling rates and found that this leads to an interesting phenomenon known as dynamic self-organization, where the engine's response to fluctuating potentials changes over time. We've verified our results through numerical simulations in both Markovian and non-Markovian environments. Overall, we've found that the engines within this novel framework can exhibit a wide range of behaviors, from Brownian dynamics to complex bistable patterns, all powered by the difference in inelastic electron tunneling rates. In recent years, specialized hardware has been designed to accelerate the generalized convolution operation, a key component of signal processing and several machine learning algorithms. Multiple optimized algorithms have been developed to execute generalized convolution efficiently, some of which leverage Compressed Sensing techniques. These algorithms typically rely on the normalization of input data by its mean and variance. This paper explores an alternative approach that bypasses such data normalization, relying instead on a simplified calculation that exploits properties of the Pearson distribution. This method is then augmented with a CS framework for optimal parameter selection. Our approach consistently outperforms traditional algorithms in computational speed while maintaining comparable or improved accuracy. Additionally, our results demonstrate that the generalized convolution operation can be efficiently executed at the hardware level using a dedicated VLSI prototype. This implementation outperforms software implementations by a significant margin, achieving a 30 times faster completion time with comparable error rates. Furthermore, our CS-enhanced algorithm outperforms conventional methods in both software and hardware implementations by substantial margins, with a 20 and 166 times faster completion time respectively, while maintaining comparable error rates. This approach can be scaled for use in a range of practical projects. HD80606b, a planet that orbits a G-type star about 84.8 light-years from Earth, has one of the most extended and unusual orbital patterns among the planets discovered so far. This research aims to update the official timing of HD80606b's closest approach to its star using a unique data analysis from various telescope observations. By incorporating data from different sources, including the Kepler space mission and ground-based observations using the I2S network of telescopes, we have successfully updated the official timing of HD80606b's closest approach, which is now accurate to a precision of about 0.0003 days. In the field of vehicle autonomy, push-off events following yield signs pose a challenge for autonomous vehicles. The push-off scenario requires swift reaction to avoid colliding with other vehicles, which is difficult even for experienced drivers. We simulate this scenario in a digital environment to determine whether autonomous vehicles can respond adequately. Our simulation indicates that when pushed, the vehicle's longitudinal velocity significantly changes, leading to a large variation in the push-off point. As a result, we suggest that the push-off event likely ends when the vehicle's wheels lose contact with the ground, which is influenced by factors such as the push force and the vehicle's mass. To determine the lateral velocity of the vehicle upon push-off, we analyze the pusher's motion and find that it is largely unaffected by factors such as the pusher's speed before the push and his weight, whereas the vehicle's lateral velocity is largely unimportant. We create a model to calculate the push-off time and find that it closely matches the outcomes of our simulation. Our study's findings serve as a benchmark for more advanced machine learning algorithms, with the ultimate goal being to transition to more sophisticated models in the future. It is found that a relatively basic linear regression model is sufficient for predicting the push-off time, which indicates that this problem is generally well-understood. Additionally, we make public the push-off dataset that we used for our training and validation processes. Our code for running the simulation and training the model can also be accessed through our GitHub repository, allowing others to replicate our study's methods and findings. We hope that our study will contribute to the development of more effective algorithms for autonomous vehicle operation. In particular, we believe that our work on push-off events will ultimately contribute to improving reaction times in autonomous vehicles. In vision-based robotic navigation, the capability to use past experiences significantly enhances performance.  Most robotic methods treat memory as a means to quantify experience, disregarding its content.  In contrast, we propose MemoNav, a model that extracts and employs insightful remembrances in visual navigation.  By leveraging a graph-based map and episodic memory, MemoNav identifies and incorporates meaningful experiences to accomplish a task, such as navigating to an unseen location.  To accomplish this, MemoNav employs a candidate generation module that identifies comparable areas between the target and past visits, then applies a criterion to determine which remembrance to select and integrate into the current map.  Through testing on a dataset of real-world indoor scenes, MemoNav demonstrated more effective navigation and reduced memory errors compared to existing approaches.  Additionally, human evaluations confirmed that MemoNav's remembrances more accurately reflected real-world experiences.  A video showcasing MemoNav's capabilities in visual navigation is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U3kxkx4yQ4g. This research develops a new concept, dynamic hypergraphs, integrating the flexibility of temporal networks into the structure of attemporal hypergraphs. It integrates the ability to add, remove, and modify connections within a network over time. An algorithm is presented to establish a mapping of dynamic hypergraphs to attractor networks, preserving the temporal sequence of interactions. Furthermore, a method is described to approximate the dynamic hypergraphs using temporary clusters, which group nodes based on past associations. An evaluation of this mapping and approximation algorithm is conducted through both real and artificial case studies in fields such as biology and finance. They demonstrate that the algorithms successfully capture the underlying structure of complex networks, enabling effective recovery of the dynamic hypergraphs and accurate classification of temporal sequences. Moreover, the precision of the algorithms is shown to improve significantly with the density of the network. These findings have potential applications in fields such as systems biology and financial portfolio analysis. Code for these procedures is available on GitHub at the specified link. Additionally, a detailed tutorial on the implementation of the algorithms can be found on UMAP's website under tutorials. Building upon previous research on operator expansion, this study further develops theory and practical applications of a novel technique - a twisted Verlinde algorithm - for a broad class of locally supersymmetric theories in higher dimensions. This involves a detailed analysis of the operator product expansion, correction terms, and weight spaces within a twisted formalism. Notably, the twisted algebra and clean sector structure are foundational components of this theory. By examining specific examples, such as free bosons and fermions, as well as Yang-Mills theories and conformal theories, we demonstrate the efficacy of the twisted algorithm in calculating branching functions and degenerate branching functions. Furthermore, this formalism has practical applications in computing Casimir operators and entropy of BPS states. A key outcome of this research is the derivation of a formula for degenerate branching functions in four-dimensional $\mathcal N=8$ supergravity, which is a seminal finding in the field. Additionally, this study also addresses general concepts and their mathematical implications. In particular, the study connects the twisted algorithm to established methods like local operators and their correlation functions, and explores the role of weight spaces in factorizing the operator product expansion. This connection is particularly evident in the analysis of a free boson and a free fermion. Finally, this study initiates and paves the way for future research in algebraic and combinatorial fields by addressing questions related to the twisted algebra, clean sector structure, and weight spaces. These questions include but are not limited to: what constitutes the general structure of these sectors and weight spaces and what rules govern their interactions? What kind of algebra underlies the twisted formalism? What are the fundamental properties of the primary fields in this framework and how do they relate to each other? All these open issues and others need to be addressed; however, the twisted algorithm shows significant promise in resolving them and this study represents a significant step in that direction. The occurrence of oscillatory and tip-dividing instabilities during dynamic fracture in brittle materials can't be overlooked. When stress waves faster than the fracture process reach the crack, these instabilities often emerge, resulting in the propagation of new cracks along the original fracture face. A proposed framework combines linear elasticity with a weakly nonlinear fracture energy to study this phenomenon, taking into account the inherent material length scales associated with fracture. By analyzing the governing equations, researchers identified both a stress-driven oscillatory instability and a fracture-energy-driven tip-dividing instability. Through numerical simulations, the roles of inherent material length scales were explored, as well as the impact of an external stress wave on a pre-existing crack, revealing a critical threshold above which these instabilities become dominant. The effects of crack history and initial stress conditions on the formation of new cracks were also examined, as well as the possibility of coexistence and patterns resulting from the complex interplay of crack lines. This work lays the foundation for a new understanding of oscillatory and tip-dividing instabilities, their causes and consequences, and the resulting intricate fracture patterns. Furthermore, researchers successfully produced some of the observed fracture patterns experimentally using quartz, an achievement that validates the theoretical framework and provides a pathway for future studies. The developed framework not only explains various intrinsic length scales associated with fracture but also offers a versatile tool for investigating how material length scales influence fracture patterns. By adjusting material parameters within realistic ranges, researchers can reproduce a wide array of experimental observations, as seen in various materials like polymers and metals. The proposed framework thus holds great potential for studying dynamic fracture in a broad range of materials. Lastly, researchers have demonstrated that by combining their length-scale-aware approach with existing phase-field methods, they can successfully reproduce both the oscillatory and tip-dividing instabilities, as well as more intricate fracture patterns, using an advanced numerical method. This method, which incorporates fracture energy and micromanagement of crack faces, enables precise control over the inherent material length scales associated with fracture, resulting in a complete reproduction of the fracture process. The successful implementation of this advanced numerical method paves the way for utilizing an extended phase-field approach to simulate and understand the complex dynamics of fracture in a diverse range of materials. Furthermore, researchers have shown that by incorporating the effects of shear modulus on fracture, they can successfully predict the presence of an intrinsic fracture length scale, a finding that validates their length-scale-aware approach and provides a foundation for further study.
