In finite-state communication systems, the transmitter typically has knowledge of the channel conditions and receives feedback from the receiver. However, in standard approaches, the encoder and decoder lack insight into the communication channel's state. This research closes this knowledge gap by designing encoders and decoders that operate within finite-state Markov chains, resulting in optimal communication performance as evidenced by achievable rates under various channel conditions. We also introduce a universal encoding method that is applicable to any finite-state channel, offering a convenient solution. Furthermore, our findings reveal specific conditions under which the standard ARQ protocol achieves the maximum error probability and illustrate a scenario in which the standard approach still offers a significant benefit. Finally, we examine how our results generalize to channels with multiple input variables. Experimental data collected from randomly generated channels in dimensions four and eight confirm our theoretical predictions. The study offers a thorough investigation of the maximum rates and minimal error probabilities achievable through finite-state communication, providing new insights and practical solutions. A theoretical model using the attractive Rashba Hubbard framework on a two-dimensional square lattice is developed to simulate spin-orbit coupling.  This model simultaneously incorporates both Rashba and Dresselhaus spin-orbit coupling effects, with their combination equivalent to a effective spin-orbit coupling of a circular orbit.  By applying the Kubo formula and functional derivative method, a spin su(2) topological insulator's spin Hall conductivity and Berry curvature are calculated.  Furthermore, a mean-field analysis of this model as a Fermi superfluid using the Rashba Hubbard model reveals a superfluid and topological insulator coexistence phase when the Rashba-Dresselhaus coupling exceeds a certain threshold and also in the strong spin-orbit coupling limit.  By applying the same functional derivative method used for the insulating phase, a spin su(2) topological superfluid's spin Hall conductivity and Berry curvature are calculated for the superfluid phase.  Two possible experimental indications of spin su(2) topological superfluidity are proposed.  Additionally, a proposed experiment to create and study a spin su(2) topological superfluid in an optical lattice is outlined.  Based on this model, a spin su(2) topological superfluid's Berry phase and spin Hall conductivity can be observed as a collective phenomenon.  Specifically, this experiment could demonstrate the existence of a $\pi$ Berry phase and associated spin Hall effect for a number of electrons less than or equal to 10.

In quantum physics, the concept of intrinsically linked coordinates has significant implications. These unique coordinates, which are essential in fermi statistics, appear in fermi pairs, and are closely related to the concept of exchange in molecules. Furthermore, they play a crucial role in the development of modern computational chemistry methods used to calculate molecular properties. This paper proposes a multi-threaded Framework for Energy-efficient Neuromorphic Architectures (FENEA), a SystemC-based toolset that supports the concurrent development of simulating neuromorphic architectures in hardware-in-the-loop environments. The framework consists of three primary modules: the model generator, the simulator, and the testbench. The model generator employs C++ to create multi-threaded models of artificial neural networks, while the simulator and testbench modules leverage SystemC for concurrent operation. The effectiveness of FENEA was demonstrated through the simulation of a binary classification task using a thread-safe model of a spiking neural network, thereby facilitating the identification of synchronization issues arising from thread sharing and data dependencies. The proposed framework serves as a resource for developing and evaluating neuromorphic computing architectures, offering a versatile tool for exploring various design approaches and evaluation metrics. FENEA is open-source and accessible at https://github.com/SDSoC-FEA/fenea. The source code includes a full implementation of the tool's functionality, as well as detailed user guides and documentation available at https://fenea.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html. The framework supports multiple design parameters, including network topologies, thread configuration, and memory management policies, enabling designers to systematically evaluate and optimize neuromorphic computing architectures according to specific application requirements. One such case study involved evaluating the performance of a spiking neural network model on an FPGA platform, where the model's thread configuration was optimized for maximum accuracy in a binary classification task. The proposed framework serves as a versatile platform for developing and evaluating novel neuromorphic computing architectures, thereby facilitating their practical application in real-world settings. Traditional machine learning models are limited when it comes to making absolute certain predictions, as their outcomes are often clouded by doubt. In contrast, humans are capable of forming definite conclusions based on uncertain premises. For instance, if a doctor suspects a patient's symptoms point to a particular disease but is not entirely sure, they can still conclude the patient needs medical attention with certainty. We refer to this form of reasoning as decision under quantified ambiguity, or duqa for short. In this study, we acquire a new model of duqa reasoning, which we call indecision forests. Informed by game theory and the principles of first-order logic with common knowledge, our approach is the first of its kind to develop a formal representation of duqa reasoning. Our key contribution is an algorithm that generates an indecision forest - a specific type of probabilistic classifier - from a set of training data. Through experimentation, we demonstrate that forests trained on a specific dataset can overcome a specific shortcut in reasoning known as the lottery ticket problem. Ultimately, the principles underlying our work have far-reaching implications for a wide range of fields, including artificial intelligence, epistemology, and political theory. As a result, our method offers a novel way to tackle challenging decision-making tasks that are inherently uncertain and provides a new framework for artificial intelligence to model absolute certain outcomes based on uncertain premises. At the same time, our work also highlights the distinct features of duqa reasoning that set it apart from more conventional forms of machine learning. In software testing, instructors can utilize two approaches to educate students:  (1) conceptual feedback focusing on general ideas, or (2) detailed feedback covering specific criteria.  This study analyzed the effectiveness of these methods among 96 undergraduate students in Turkey.  The students were divided into two groups, one receiving conceptual feedback and the other receiving detailed feedback, as they learned about software testing.  Both groups took a pre-test and a post-test on the same material.  The results showed that students receiving conceptual feedback performed better on the post-test, required fewer repetitions of the same course, and demonstrated a deeper understanding of software testing, all measured through practical exercises, a multiple-choice quiz, and a written exam.  The students receiving conceptual feedback also expressed more confident answers, according to the Hake index.  Additionally, the instructor provided students with more relevant and actionable feedback in the conceptual feedback group, as subjectively assessed.  The study highlights that conceptual feedback leads to better academic outcomes, requires fewer resources to deliver, and results in more efficient teaching, all supporting its use as a testing education method. In this study, we used concept analysis to break down a prediction into more interpretable components, but found the existing method fell short due to its limited ability to generalize. This led us to develop a new approach, ExpressNet, which merges concept analysis with inductive logic programming (ILP) to generate human-friendly explanations for classification predictions. By treating concepts as unknown variables and using instance data to learn their boundaries, ILP helps pinpoint specific instances that define each concept. However, this method faces challenges such as identifying global concepts that encompass local patterns. To overcome this, ILP integrates with a neural network that filters out irrelevant instances, allowing us to identify stable concepts that generalize across different datasets and perturbations. We establish a universal framework for $\alpha$-attractor inflation models that are predictable and expandable, thereby enabling scientists to make accurate predictions regarding future inflation and the characteristics of primordial black holes. The parameter $\alpha$ in these models determines the rate of expansion, and we are able to derive this parameter through a singular transformation, thereby simplifying the original $\alpha$-attractor equations. By analyzing the evolution of the Hubble rate and the primordial spectral index, we demonstrate that only a narrow range of $\alpha$ values leads to inflationary scenarios that are consistent with observations. Furthermore, we show that models with $\alpha < 0.01$ give rise to universe ages that are in agreement with estimates based on cosmic microwave background radiation, and we predict additional stages of expansion followed by a long period of slow-roll inflation. In many of these scenarios, the final stages of expansion result in the creation of primordial black holes, and we calculate the corresponding mass ranges $10^{-16}M_\odot \lesssim M_{\rm PBH} \lesssim M_{\rm EW}$. Additionally, we find that the LIGO bounds on dark matter in the form of primordial black holes are exceeded by masses from the early stages of $\alpha$-attractor expansion, and we estimate these masses to be in the range $10^{-12}M_\odot \lesssim M_{\rm PBH} \lesssim 10^{-6}M_\odot$. In a number of cases, these primordial black holes would have evaporated during the early stages of the radiation era, thereby their masses would have been limited by the mass of electrons ($\sim 10^{-13}M_\odot$). Finally, we propose an approach for identifying particles produced by short-lived stages of radial expansion, and we suggest that future projects such as the Large Hadron Collider could potentially detect these particles. In a number of cases, these particles would have masses comparable to the mass of mesons, and we outline a detection strategy for these particles as well as ones produced by a quasi-stable stage of lateral expansion, in which their masses would be limited by the mass of baryons. In this detection strategy, we propose the use of beam dump experiments, as well as heavy particle decays, as promising avenues for identifying these particles as signals of additional, long since completed stages of expansion in the universe's history. We present an investigation into how researchers formulate queries to gather information for their publications. A thorough reading of over 55,000 academic papers in the fields of computer science and biomedicine enabled us to sample 442 questions from 122 scientists. These queries were examined in terms of their content, and the responses were evaluated in relation to how they were implemented. We analyzed the characteristics of research-related queries, the language used to formulate them, and the logic that governs their structure, as well as the data sources consulted and the search engines utilized for information retrieval. The distinctions in query formulation logic exhibited by individual researchers were found to be consistent, allowing scientists to develop their own distinct search methodologies. These observations, supported by concrete examples, demonstrate that the information-seeking behavior of researchers can be viewed as a manifestation of their expertise, much like their writing and collaboration styles. We hope that our data and analysis will facilitate the development of systems that learn from and adapt to the information-seeking behavior of their users. Notably, a neutrino type II instability can also give rise to a variety of non-spherical and turbulent patterns, particularly when neutrino optics are considered in three-dimensional simulations.

The study demonstrated the effectiveness of data refinement in rs-fMRI analysis for ADHD diagnosis. Additionally, by projecting brain activity onto a behavioral space, we found that ADHD-like patterns are characterized by reduced activity in regions such as the prefrontal cortex and increased activity in the default mode network. These findings align with established ADHD theories. The complexity of this model is reduced and it can be studied under a two-time scale framework, where the fast and slow time scales are analyzed separately. The results show that the disease transmission rates in the fast and slow time scales are independent of the district in question and can be calculated as a product of the basic epidemic criterion and spatial diffusion rates, which are also independent of the district. In everyday communication, acronyms and abbreviations are employed as shorthand for comprehensive phrases, whereas "buzzwords" serve as concise versions of longer expressions. Conversely, the extensive use of acronyms and "buzzwords" leads to confusion, rendering their comprehension crucial for effective human-machine interaction. To address the recognition and clarification of acronyms and "buzzwords," we introduce MadDog, a cutting-edge online platform that facilitates seamless integration with diverse applications via its API. MadDog boasts an integrated dictionary encompassing 2.5 million entries, encompassing acronyms, "buzzwords," and their expansions across English, Spanish, French, and German languages. Furthermore, the platform offers the functionality to ascertain the meanings of acronyms and "buzzwords" in user-submitted texts, enabling real-time clarification through pop-up windows or web browser extensions. Orchestration of the system occurs at Google's Cloud infrastructure, ensuring high scalability and efficiency in processing requests. Evaluation experiments demonstrate MadDog's capabilities in processing thousands of queries per second on a single node. Our evaluation also highlights MadDog's superiority over competing systems in acronym clarification accuracy, with an overall error rate of 8.64%. Additionally, the system exhibits adaptability across diverse domains through the application of our automated acronym recognition tool, ACR. This tool has been utilized in numerous research projects and can be freely accessed via the MadDog API. To facilitate user understanding, we have developed a demo page illustrating MadDog's features in user-driven acronym clarification. Furthermore, the system enables developers to integrate MadDog into custom applications using example code samples available on our website. In summary, MadDog serves as a comprehensive online system for acronym clarification, offering a suite of sophisticated features, a substantial dictionary, and exceptional efficiency in processing capabilities. Through its adaptable technology, MadDog empowers diverse applications with seamless integration, enhancing human-machine communication by ensuring the effective recognition and clarification of acronyms and "buzzwords." Finally, the system promotes user comprehension through visual aids and clarification mechanisms. MadDog is open-source, providing API access and accompanying source code to support researchers and developers in their academic and practical endeavors related to acronym recognition and clarification. This system aims to promote efficient knowledge sharing among researchers in this field. Knowledge shared by the community can be freely utilized, and we encourage researchers to utilize MadDog in their studies. The system is now available for public use at madDog.org. In oscillatory media, pacemaker-generated waves exhibit a unique characteristic, where a central complex pattern arises from minimal initial disturbances. This phenomenon has been observed in various biological systems, such as the intestinal muscle, where it plays a significant role in regulating the digestive system's motility. Prior research has primarily focused on analyzing the dynamics of pacemaker-generated waves using numerical methods and modeling techniques. However, these approaches often result in complex, difficult-to-interprete equations that require time-consuming numerical simulations. In contrast, this study proposes a group of analytical estimations for the velocity of pacemaker-generated waves, where the accuracy of these estimations depends solely on a few key parameters and can be solved using elementary mathematics. Furthermore, the proposed estimations exhibit excellent agreement with numerical simulations and experimental results, confirming their precision and utility. This research demonstrates that the velocity of pacemaker-generated waves can be accurately estimated using a simple formula based on the distance between the pacemaker and farthest active elements, as well as the time it takes for signal propagation and processing within the pacemaker system. Importantly, this study reveals that the velocity of these waves is not solely determined by the pacemaker system's frequency but is also significantly influenced by its response time, an insight that has important practical implications. Ultimately, this research confirms that the velocity of pacemaker-generated waves can be accurately estimated using straightforward analytical formulas, providing a more efficient and accurate alternative to numerical methods and modeling techniques. Additionally, these estimations offer valuable insights into the functional properties of biological oscillatory systems, where the velocity of these waves may serve as an indicator of optimal wave propagation and the integration of pacemaker-generated rhythms. Lastly, this study demonstrates that the analytical estimations of velocity can be generalized to a broad range of applications, where they can be utilized to predict and describe the dynamics of rhythmic motions in oscillatory media. This research will enable scientists to develop more accurate and efficient numerical simulation algorithms, ultimately facilitating a deeper understanding of the underlying biological systems and their applications in solving real-world problems. Consequently, this research will open up new avenues for the effective numerical simulation of pacemaker-generated waves and other rhythmic phenomena in oscillatory media. At the same time, it will create novel opportunities for the practical implementation of these models, where the velocity of these waves can be leveraged to achieve tangible results and improve existing solutions. This research will therefore contribute to the advancement of numerical methods and modeling techniques, where the analysis of pacemaker-generated waves plays a significant role in understanding the dynamics of oscillatory media.

We investigate a variety of classical algorithms that can compute an approximation of the von Neumann entropy for a quantum state, these algorithms operate under conditions of limited access to the state and are subject to noise during query execution. By studying these algorithms, we demonstrate that there is a threshold of query complexity - however low it may be - below which it is not possible to accurately estimate the entropy of a quantum state, this threshold applies even in the case where the state is perfectly known in advance. This result is a manifestation of a broader principle known as the sublinear threshold hypothesis, a principle which we validate in this study by combining it with known findings on quantum data analysis. By crossing over into the quantum realm, we study a variety of algorithms that can approximate the entropy using quantum queries, these algorithms are found to be either equivalent to a simple black-box approach or to a more sophisticated oracle that utilizes logarithmic access to the state, this latter oracle being found to be indispensable for accurate entropy estimation. Ultimately, we identify a delicate interplay between the resources required for entropy estimation - a relationship between the depth, width, and query complexity of the algorithm - a relationship which holds both in the noisy and noiseless query models. This study is the first to comprehensively examine the resources required for entropy estimation in the quantum setting. By contrast, we examine a different metric in the classical setting, specifically reverse Shennon information, and establish a threshold of query complexity - however low it may be - below which it is not possible to accurately estimate this metric, this threshold applies even in the case where the related distribution is known in advance through a sample. In pulmonary medicine, documenting chronic conditions via International Classification of Diseases (ICD) coding is essential, yet currently cumbersome and technology limited. Due to its manual nature, documentation is often incomplete, leading to costly data quality issues. A proposed system aims to rectify this by automatically filling gaps in existing data, improving overall completeness and precision through semi-supervised learning techniques, specifically label propagation and adaptation. By employing a multi-coded, semi-supervised approach, the system can identify unclassified patients and fill missing codes with relevant ICDS, enhancing clinical data and and and and overall treatment efficiency. A database containing 456,689 patient records and corresponding ICD codes was used to test the system's effectiveness, yielding impressive results with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.955 for ten most frequently used ICDS and top 100 chronic conditions. Following thorough validation, the top three performing codes showed a substantial increase in accuracy, reaching 0.977 for the first code, 0.962 for the second, and 0.949 for the third. A comprehensive reliability analysis using Cohen's kappa showed strong agreement among the top ten codes, averaging 0.881 and as high as 0.927 for code number five. A subsequent evaluation with ten domain experts further demonstrated the system's clinical value, resulting in an average ranking of 2.08 out of a possible ten for code number one and a top ten ranking for all codes except number eight. A subsequent sensitivity and variability analysis confirmed the system's robustness and ability to consistently and accurately classify codes under a wide range of parameter settings, also revealing inherent variability in human coding practices that the system aims to standardize and improve. A theoretical cost-benefit analysis estimated a potential annual savings of $0.76 per patient due to reduced documentation costs, translating to $337,652 for a database of 445,691 patients. A subsequent study protocol was proposed, aiming to further validate and refine the system in a controlled clinical setting, addressing existing concerns and limitations of the study, primarily related to using simulated missing data rather than real codes. It is anticipated that the developed semi-supervised system will significantly improve clinical data quality and precision, yielding substantial economic benefits while standardizing and aligning human coding practices with the International Classification of Diseases. By examining the properties of these anomalies in relation to those of known anomalies from 2015-2017, we seek to understand any systematic patterns or variations. A comparison of the anomalous characteristics shows them to be equivalent in terms of location, magnitude, and time-based displacement in the Jupiter-like field, but displaying distinct differences in the Gaia-like field. Interestingly, the prime field's anomalies exhibit an overall 7.5% occurrence rate, suggesting under-detection of this phenomenon in the publicly available 2018 data. By comparing the prime field's anomaly rate to that of the 2015-2017 dataset, we infer the existence of an entity we've dubbed "X," which is responsible for creating this phenomenon, having a characteristic size of ~0.16aru'' and a mass of ~4.2M_Jupiter, capable of causing a 0.7% change in the anomaly occurrence rate for each unit change in its size, while also affecting the probability of detecting an anomaly by ~7.5% as well as its overall rate, regardless of the anomaly's size, in the Jupiter-like field. However, "X" does not contribute to changes in the Gaia-like field's anomaly occurrence rate. Additionally, we've discovered that the prime field's anomalies display a more even distribution of their center-of-mass motion in relation to the telescope's field of view, suggesting that "X" might not be confined to a specific area and might be self-organizing, explaining this pattern in the data. Furthermore, we've found evidence of non-gravitational factors affecting the anomalies' motion in the Gaia-like field, which might be attributed to the presence of "X" as well as other entities producing microlensing signals, contributing to this phenomenon. Lastly, we've determined the likelihood of detecting anomalies towards the Galactic center over the course of the 2018 season to be ~80%, implying a high likelihood of identifying "X"-related signals in data collected from this area during this time period. Ultimately, we propose several methods by which further research on these anomalies can continue. Additionally, we've compiled a comprehensive list of 119 anomalies from the 2018 season towards the Galactic bulge, which can be accessed through the KMTNet website at the following link: http://kmtnet.net

Three-dimensional object rendering relies on accurate surface area mapping to generate realistic visual effects, but solving inverse problems for real-world rendering is complicated due to non-differentiable shadow calculations in traditional rendering algorithms, limiting their application in differentiable learning methods. A new, differentiable shadow computation approach has been developed, allowing non-hierarchical, differentiable surface area mapping models to directly handle occlusions and unknown boundaries in real-world rendering. This innovative method has been designed for solving critical 3D object shape recovery problems in real-world rendering contexts, like human body shape recovery from one or multiple images, and can be readily adapted to other inverse rendering problems, such as material and lighting estimation. Experimental results from real-world datasets and simulations confirm the efficacy of this novel method, surpassing state-of-the-art surface area mapping models in real-world rendering scenarios. A open-source implementation of this work has been made available.

An algorithmic approach is developed to create a uniform spanning tree randomly from a connected graph with n vertices. Subsequently, a perfect matching is generated within this tree to obtain a uniform spanning tree through a series of transformations. Notably, the method provides a means of generating arbitrary spanning trees in a connected graph with a specified property by first extending the graph to include vertices with the desired characteristic. The method's efficiency is supported by asymptotic analysis, revealing an average number of operations proportional to n for generating a uniform spanning tree. The flow of heat within a stationary bed of particles, typically found in solar receivers and heat exchangers, is often disregarded due to an erroneous assumption that conduction is negligible compared to convective transport. However, for certain geometries and operating conditions, this assumption is incorrect, leading to an underestimation of the thermal resistance offered by the particle bed. As a result, designs become either too large or unable to dissipate heat effectively, posing significant problems. This study demonstrates the validity of an analytical equation for the thermal resistance of a particle bed by imaging its temperature distribution using rapid magnetic resonance imaging. The experiment involved probing a bed of 1 mm diameter glass particles, 0.3 meters in depth, while heated from below. The observed temperature gradient in the particles was documented, and the data matched well with the predictions of an analytical formula, thereby validating its use in solid particle beds. The effect of varying the particle diameter, bed depth, and heat source location was also examined. The outcome of this research supports numerical models, confirming that high-performance solar receivers can benefit from accounting for the thermal conductivity of the particle bed. This finding holds potential for applications in fields such as solar energy, heat exchangers, and the study of natural environments like dunes. Moreover, the employed MRI technique offers promising opportunities for the in situ visualization of thermal phenomena in various systems. The analysis presented here serves as a general guideline, applicable to a broad range of particle beds and operating conditions. The methodology can be adapted for in situ imaging of particle beds in reactors, receivers, and other equipment, providing direct visual evidence to support design optimizations. Lastly, the adaptation of this technique could facilitate in situ monitoring of operational systems, including online validation of numerical models and simulations. This could lead to better-designed natural environments, efficient solar collectors, and effectively operating industrial processes, all made possible by a deeper understanding of the complex interactions between solid particles and the fluid that surrounds them. As a result, the thermal resistance offered by a particle bed becomes a valuable asset, rather than an obstacle to be overcome. The data collected here can be used to optimize the performance of solar power tiles, industrial heat exchangers, and other systems by taking full advantage of the thermal conductivity provided by the particle bed. Furthermore, this research has significant implications for the design of more efficient solar collectors, effective industrial heat exchangers, and natural environments, by incorporating the thermal conductivity of the particle bed. Building on previous work by Bedrossian, Masmoudi, and Mazzulini, we establish a dynamic system that governs the long-term behavior of disturbances to couple flow in two-dimensional complex fluids. We demonstrate the existence of non-trivial traveling waves within this system and show they persist under weak dissipation. Furthermore, we find that as weak dissipation is introduced, these traveling waves move at fast speeds, resulting in long-term growth in the associated disturbance. A key step in our proof involves creating a "bad energies" framework, which allows us to analyze high-frequency behavior, as well as develop a "bootstrap scheme," to capture long-term evolution in the disturbance. We also introduce a new mathematical tool - the "biais energy" - to describe how the disturbance evolves in space and time, all while maintaining sharp control over the highest frequency components. A related result shows that as the shear rate increases, the distance between nearby Couette flows grows, leading to increasingly chaotic behavior. We achieve this by cleverly manipulating Bedrossian-Masmoudi-Mazzulini's "biais energy" framework and applying a technical argument first presented by Chaudret, Masmoudi, and Mazzulini.

The consequence is that elements of A are confined to a linear pattern defined by b + B, where b belongs to A and B's maximal cardinality does not exceed k/4. This simplification yields an alternative proof of Szemeredi's sumset conjecture for k smaller than 2.02 binomial k choose 2. 

Furthermore, we demonstrate a more general concept, referred to as the Freiman holographic principle. This principle asserts that for any subsets A and B of integers, the inner sumset A⋅B corresponds directly to a corresponding inner sumset B⋅A, provided that both A⋅B and B⋅A's maximal cardinalities do not exceed k. In response to an inquiry from Terence Tao, we also show that A⋅B may not necessarily equal B⋅A for all possible subsets A and B of integers, regardless of their sizes. Ultimately, this Freiman holographic principle serves as the foundation for our abstract theorem.

This robust version asserts that a subset A of integers with a sum set m(A), where the cardinality of A and m(A) combined equals k, is confined to a linear pattern defined by b + B, where b belongs to A and B's maximal cardinality does not exceed k/4. A clear limit exists on the number of subgroups a finite group can have, limited by $2^{2\frac{\log |G|}{\log 2}+o(\log |G|)}$ count of subgroups, where $o(\log |G|)$ represents smaller order terms. This limit was first identified by Tsaranukha in 1977 with the same order of magnitude, now widely accepted in the field. Our research verifies Tsaranukha's finding and provides a clear explanation for the finding. Additionally, a detailed analysis was conducted on the possible values of the subgroup count and the possible subgroups with their orders less than half of the group's order. It was found that the number of subgroups with orders less than half of the group's order is less than $|G|^{\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon}$. Consequently, the number of subgroups with orders less than half of the group's order and index less than half of the group's order is less than $|G|^{\frac{3}{4}+\epsilon}$. These results were first identified in the paper and are now widely accepted in the field. It was further found that a finite group $G$ with more than $|G|^{\frac{3}{4}+\epsilon}$ subgroups of index less than half of the group's order must have a subgroup of index less than half of the group's order within another subgroup of index less than half of the group's order. This discovery led to the classification theorem for finite groups with the subgroup count close to Tsaranukha's limit, and also led to the discovery of the smallest finite nonabelian group, which has a subgroup count close to Tsaranukha's limit. It was further found that a finite group $G$ with a subgroup count close to Tsaranukha's limit must have a nilpotent subgroup with index less than half of the group's order. By combining these results, it was found that a finite group $G$ with a subgroup count close to Tsaranukha's limit must have a nilpotent subgroup with index less than half of the group's order. This discovery led to the classification theorem for finite groups with a nilpotent subgroup with index less than half of the group's order. It was further found that a finite group $G$ with a subgroup count close to Tsaranukha's limit must have a cyclic subgroup with index less than half of the group's order.

In this paper, we reframe the challenge of reducing false positives as a binary classification task and employ an unconventional approach, or 'hard negative mining,' to enhance model discrimination. Our research suggests that light primordial black holes may continue to exist and their radio emissions could serve as cosmic background radiation at least up to an energy of $\sim 10^{-14}$ Ergs. This energy range falls within the reach of Square Kilometre Array telescopes. It's possible that background signals from these holes could be misinterpreted as coming from young neutron stars or pulsar wind nebulae. To estimate the background intensity, we used the primordial black hole abundance metrics related to the dark matter fraction and the scale of large-scale structure. This led to a lower limit on the number of these holes per unit energy range of $\mathcal{N}(E)\simeq 10^{10}\mathcal{G}\mathrm{cm}^{-3}\mathrm{Erg}^{-1}$, where $\mathcal{G}$ is the fraction of dark matter these holes comprise and $E$ is the energy range in Ergs. To mitigate these expenses, newer approaches, such as zero-based programming, emulating bit-level operations, and tokenizing data, have incorporated additional memory or gate overhead in an attempt to decrease costs. However, these improved schemes themselves become computationally burdensome as programs increase in size. In contrast, this paper's proposed Virtual Safe Framework (VSF) achieves both efficient computational costs and sufficient function evaluation capabilities. By incorporating a specialized hardware setup, VSF's five-stage processor pipeline, and the use of a specific programming model, this paper demonstrates a substantial enhancement in evaluation costs for various functions, and even surpasses previous efficiency improvements, such as zero-based programming, in specific arithmetic operations like multiplication. The discovery of rapidly rotating hot Jupiters has led to theories of equal mass stars and planets forming close to the host star due to conservation of angular momentum. However, these stars rotate slowly, suggesting planet transfer of angular momentum. We analyzed the rotation rates of F, G, and K stars within the TIC catalog, and our results show that hot stars, particularly those in close orbit, rotate faster than expected, while those farther away rotate more slowly as expected. Additionally, there is a notable disparity in the rotation rates of solar twins when compared to randomly selected stars from the same metallicity range, indicating that planetary interaction is the most plausible explanation. If these planets are responsible, they must absorb a significant portion of the star's mechanical energy or lose momentum to some unknown mechanism. We suggest further observation of low-mass stars and planets to confirm this phenomenon and its underlying causes. To tackle the inherent data scarcity problem in personalized recommendation, several session-based recommendation models have been developed. They focus solely on the current and previous user actions, disregarding external information. This can lead to subpar internal consistency within user behavior. In an attempt to address this, we propose a new session-based recommendation model called Self-Guided Session-based Recommendation (SGSR). It combines both current and historical behavior, utilizing a self-guided learning approach to enhance internal consistency. This model achieves improved performance by employing a two-stage method that includes graph co-training and self-supervision. The latter leverages an internally-generated pseudo-label guide, obtained from the model's initial training stage. Experimental results demonstrate superior performance of SGSR over cutting-edge session-based recommendation models on real-world datasets. Quantum bits in silicon have garnered significant attention due to their potential for robust and efficient execution of quantum algorithms. A unique characteristic of silicon quantum bits, known as valley degree freedom, must be carefully controlled in order to meet the strict constraints of quantum computing. However, the process of valley interaction in silicon remains poorly understood at a molecular level. This study employs a advanced superconducting quantum dot SQUID sensor to accurately measure the valley interaction in silicon. We've discovered that valley interaction in silicon is significantly influenced by interface impurities and crystal defects near the interface. A highly tunable interface impurity can induce valley mixing through its electrostatic field, while defects can induce spin-valley coupling through magnetic interactions. This represents the first documented instance of spin-valley coupling in silicon quantum bits and holds significant potential for the development of efficient spin-valley transducers. Furthermore, this study showcases the exceptional sensitivity of SQUID sensors in measuring minute magnetic fields generated by quantum bits. The research also highlights the potential of using silicon quantum bits in highly accurate magnetic sensing applications. This technique allows us to map charge conduction by applying an electric field to a material using a nanosecond laser pulse, and measuring the resulting current in space with a femtosecond laser pulse. This technique could be further refined to map materials with more complex charge conduction characteristics by analyzing the spatial and temporal distribution of current. To mitigate these toxic effects, researchers have investigated the problem of detecting misogynous text in Arabic, but it remains an open challenge due to the language's complex writing system and the homogeneity of certain Arabic characters. Our work addresses this challenge by developing a novel dataset of 3090 sentences, annotated as misogynous or neutral, and a corresponding model, along with a comprehensive literature review, that achieves high accuracy in detecting misogynous text and accurately categorizing its severity. Our approach combines model-based reinforcement learning and predictive control to develop resilient policies, which we demonstrate on a planet-wide transportation network and a global supply chain management system. The presentation highlights the importance of system models in learning resilient controllers and the value of modular structures in the target system model for developing robust controllers. Natural language processing, a crucial field of study, strives to comprehend text via digital analysis, ultimately extracting meaningful insights from spoken language. One key area of exploration within NLP involves text summarization, where the primary objective is to condense lengthy documents into more manageable versions while preserving core information. This paper delves into a specific approach to text summarization, focusing on an extractive method that utilizes graphs to identify crucial sentences within a document. Prior research on text summarization relied heavily on graphs, yet the selected sentences often failed to accurately represent the original content. To address this challenge, this study introduces an improved graph-based method for text summarization, optimized through a refined scoring function that generates more effective summaries. Furthermore, the proposed approach allows for the easy integration of external knowledge, enhancing performance by incorporating additional semantic analysis. Extensive evaluation of our method was conducted using commonly employed datasets and metrics, yielding superior results that outperform established state-of-the-art techniques. Lastly, the code and associated datasets have been made publicly available for further exploration.

The rendering of line maps relies on a dithering algorithm to mitigate aliasing, which might lead to uneven color distribution particularly apparent when colors are not evenly divided. When lines intersect, they can form junctions which pose an issue as they are usually represented as single entities but need to be handled as separate lines. The effective anti-aliasing algorithm we've developed addresses this challenge by treating each line as an individual entity, allowing for distinct colors on either side of the junction. We achieve this by employing a combination of spatial anti-aliasing and temporal rendering techniques. Specifically, we use a combination of two methods: Metropolis dithering and bidirectional rendering. The former allows lines to be colored based on spatial criteria, while the latter ensures consistency along the junction and incorporates neighboring pixels for alias reduction purposes. The implementation details are further discussed in section 3. The line map rendering engine we've developed can handle various line types, including the aforementioned junctions, which set it apart from competing solutions. A pulsar's accelerated particles show significant concentration in the pulsar wind zone and, in particular, within large-scale arcs or rings, which are referred to as pulsar shells. Convolutional neural networks exhibit significant potential in distinguishing global climate types from satellite images. However, training such networks without considering the effects of cloud cover and sensor variations can lead to inaccurate results. A new dataset has been proposed, comprising 275,908 images across 13 classes and 20 sensor models, to provide a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating convolutional networks in diverse climate categories. By utilizing this dataset, the performance of various convolutional networks was assessed under different sensor conditions and the resulting metrics were analyzed. Furthermore, the best practices for achieving optimal accuracy were identified, including the use of data augmentation and network optimization through batch normalization and the selection of a 50-layer network structure. A novel enhancement approach was also proposed, allowing existing models to adapt to unfamiliar sensor conditions. The widespread consensus on the need to address global warming has led to a proliferation of environmental initiatives, often taking research beyond established scientific boundaries. Various stakeholders, including non-governmental organizations, academia, and economic entities, have developed distinct societal standards for climate change communication. To bridge the gap between these separate realms, we investigate how weather-related phenomena like severe heatwaves are discussed by different groups, focusing on the linguistic markers that reflect their shared understanding of climate change. Our analysis reveals that extreme heatwaves are consistently presented as manifestations of global warming in scientific research and environmental activism, whereas economic entities tend to view them as a byproduct of climate variability, often incorporating safety and adaptability into their discourse. By examining the interactions between these societal standards, we aim to contribute to the development of effective communication strategies, helping to mitigate the perceived disconnect between the urgent need to address climate change and the perceived uncertainty of its connection to weather events. Ultimately, this research aims to enhance public awareness and understanding, resonating with the language used by key climate change stakeholders. By bridging this comprehension gap, we may foster a more unified societal standard for climate change communication, potentially leading to collective action in addressing this pressing global issue. 

\textit{Keywords: Societal standards, climate change, discourse analysis, communication strategies, extreme heatwaves, research, non-governmental organizations, economics}

One of the most fundamental and widely used techniques in machine learning is the Gradient Descent algorithm, which has numerous variants each tailored to specific problem types and structures. Despite its many adaptations, most versions of GD neglect to account for non-stationary targets, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address this limitation, we introduce an advanced algorithm known as the Organic Gradient Descent (OGD), which serves as a unified GD framework. OGD boasts three distinct features: 1) target non-stationarity is acknowledged, 2) the algorithm is fully online, and 3) it is capable of learning from a diverse set of problem types, including reinforcement learning, regression, and classification tasks. Furthermore, we establish theoretical connections between the algorithm's parameters and the learning rate, demonstrating that OGD converges to a neighborhood of the global optimum with a rate directly influenced by the problem's parameters. Our empirical evaluations illustrate the efficacy of OGD in outperforming or rivaling the performance of established methods, such as SGD, Adam, and ProxSGD, in a range of real-world experiments. Notably, OGD's success in these trials serves as a testament to the algorithm's robust generalization capabilities. Our understanding of the conditions in the intergalactic medium (IGM) is derived from observations of high-redshift quasars, which involve analyzing the absorption lines caused by interstellar clouds along the line of sight. The properties of these clouds can be inferred from a reconstruction of their underlying density energy spectrum, obtained through a mathematical formulation known as the Radial Probability Distribution (RPD). This approach, developed in a previous study, has been further enhanced in the present research by utilizing machine learning. A sophisticated neural network is trained with simulated quasar spectra, which are generated based on a model of the IGM, and the resulting trained model is then applied to observe quasar spectra to reconstruct the RPD. The accuracy of this reconstruction is quantified by analyzing the residuals and comparing them to semi-analytical models of the IGM. The inclusion of neutral hydrogen at a redshift of z~5.5, with a volume-averaged optical depth of about 0.13, is indicated as a possible explanation for the observed distortions in the IGM at very high redshifts. Additionally, the neural network is found to effectively model the observed distributions of interstellar absorption lines, which are related to the underlying density energy spectrum of these systems. The incorporation of the neural network has enabled a more precise and data-driven analysis of the IGM, which is now primarily constrained by the observed quasar spectra, rather than semi-analytical models. The resulting more accurate quasar spectra provide essential data for understanding the IGM and its associated neutral hydrogen at very high redshifts. Recent breakthroughs in large language models have transformed the field of artificial intelligence, particularly in processing natural language. These models, designed to generate human-like text, have found extensive application in chatbots and are now being used in various domains, including customer support, education, and entertainment. However, the majority of these models are limited to specific domains and cannot engage in more complex, role-defined conversations. In this research, we present a framework that leverages the capabilities of 21st-century language models to create a sophisticated, role-defined conversation system supporting an arbitrary number of roles. To achieve this, we develop a custom set of prompts for initiating conversations, along with a series of follow-up questions to maintain the discussion. The effectiveness of our framework is demonstrated through a human evaluation, which shows significant improvement over existing models. Additionally, our framework enables a seamless transition between various roles and domains, exemplified by a "tour guide" conversation. As the universe evolves, these gravitational waves become frozen and their energy remains constant. We propose that the source of stochastic gravitational waves detected today originates from this primordial phase and the gravitational waves' memory effect, which is preserved forever. The amplitude of these damped waves corresponds to the order of $10^{-20}$ Str, and their frequency lies in the range of $10^{-18}$ to $10^{-21}$ Hz. The mechanism of gravitational waves' memory has two distinct components - the Bonazzoli-Maggiore-Ritzi memory and the de Felice-Kobayashi memory. A key objective in artificial intelligence is to derive causal relationships from limited observational data, which enables predictive capabilities. Recent breakthroughs in causal inference using neuro-symbolic approaches have shown promise to overcome traditional data limitations. Building on this progress, this research further develops an emergent modeling framework that integrates the interplay of neuro-symbolic and symbolic methods, which facilitates complex exchanges of information. Through this model, a micro-economy game is established to test causal inference, where agents with partial knowledge can either acquire the knowledge they need through a novel trading mechanism or resort to guessing. When agents engage in this trading, the emergent model enables them to exchange relevant information efficiently. As a result, this exchange enhances their collective predictive capabilities and minimizes unnecessary information exchanges, which reduces costs. A detailed analysis, supported by numerical experiments, demonstrates that the proposed trading mechanism has optimal computational properties and outperforms a comparative 'guessing' approach. Furthermore, the developed model showcases an innovative application of the emergent modeling framework in addressing artificial intelligence challenges. In the field of information retrieval and natural language processing, term forecasting is a crucial concept that underpins various applications such as document ranking and language modeling. The idea of term forecasting involves predicting when and how often a newly formed term will emerge in future data based on past usage patterns. Existing models for term forecasting are rooted in probabilistic machine learning, with a specific approach using naive Bayes to combine prior term occurrence patterns and friend relationships between terms. Although effective in general scenarios, this approach may struggle when applied to specific data sets, possibly due to its reliance on assumptions and limited integration of past contextual information into the model. To address these limitations, a new hybrid framework combines the naive Bayes model with latent data, enabling more accurate term forecasting results in specific data sets. The hybrid framework's performance was validated through exhaustive experiments on six diverse data sets, which showed a notable enhancement in prediction precision and a consistent alignment with actual term emergence patterns in five out of six data sets. The hybrid framework's performance in predicting the frequency of term encounters was also empirically confirmed. The integration of past contextual information into the model appears to play a key role in the hybrid framework's success, as evidenced by a comparison of prediction precision with and without consideration of this information. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of prediction errors in five data sets revealed a consistent shift towards more accurate estimates as the frequency of new term encounters increases, underscoring the hybrid framework's potential applications in information retrieval and natural language processing. The hybrid framework's code and six data sets are publicly available for download at https://github.com/abhishek-gupta-26/TFC. Additional details are available in Chapter 4 of the doctoral dissertation "Advanced Machine Learning Techniques for Information Retrieval" by Abhishek Gupta, published in 2021. In various biological and living organisms, differences in activity levels across membranes are common, affecting movement and interactions at cell walls. Investigating the dynamics of colloidal particles in activity gradients provides valuable insights into cellular behavior and function. This work focuses on the geometry of the activity profile and its impact on particle movements. Three distinct scenarios are examined: a constant activity level, an activity peak, and an activity gradient. Results show that a constant activity profile yields random particle movements, consistent with existing theories. In contrast, an activity peak causes the particle to orbit the peak, achieving the highest activity level. A thorough analysis of this behavior has been derived mathematically. Additionally, when an activity gradient is present, particles can move towards the active area, capturing their dynamic behavior and describing their movement in terms of the activity gradient. When the activity profile has a sine waveform, the particle exhibits periodic movement around the active area, achieving the highest activity level. This behavior has been extensively analyzed and is consistent with experimental findings for cells with oscillatory behaviors, such as those found in bacterial cell signaling pathways. Furthermore, when an activity gradient is present, particles can move towards the active area, capturing their dynamic behavior and describing their movement in terms of the activity gradient when the activity profile has an exponential waveform. This leads to the creation of an ordinary differential equation, which accurately represents the time-dependent movement of the particle in this scenario. Finally, when the activity profile has an S-shaped waveform, the particle exhibits complex movement around the active area, showing non-ergodic behavior in two-dimensional simulations. This leads to the creation of effective forces, such as those experienced by cells with intercellular junctions, which can be tested and validated in experiments. Additionally, this research provides a framework for studying the behavior of active colloids, as well as biological systems, with varying geometries of activity profiles and has potential applications in biology and medicine. It also provides a new metric for comparing the geometry of active profiles and can be extended to study the behavior of active particles under flow. Finally, this research demonstrates that the concepts of active matter and colloidal physics are interconnected and shares common tools and techniques with biology. It identifies potential areas for collaboration between biologists and physicists, as well as potential areas for clinical application, as evident in the case study of bacterial biofilms. This study centers on the development of an original algorithm for coordinating a group of autonomous drones, which work together to capture and replicate the geometric characteristics of moving objects in a confined space. The algorithm relies on a dynamic map that serves as a reference, updating and sharing information among the drones as they navigate and encounter objects in real-time. The algorithm not only ensures the drones avoid colliding with each other, but also predicts and prevents them from crashing into objects, using a robust estimation technique and correcting the drones' paths as needed. By testing this algorithm in a simulated environment, we verify its effectiveness in replicating an object's features, preserving the object's structural characteristics, and preventing collisions, at a significantly lower computational cost compared to other methods. Ultimately, our results demonstrate that this algorithm enables the drones to navigate and operate efficiently in a complex environment. This paper explores the Seidel matrix spectrum of a sequence graph, determining its eigenvalues and establishing upper limits for its prime eigenvalues. Additionally, we identify the possible prime eigenvalue sets, and calculate the maximum multiplicity of a Seidel eigenvalue. We also investigate the Seidel energy and establish maximum and minimum Seidel energies for regular sequence graphs with different degrees. Furthermore, we recreate the Hoffman polynomial and use it to determine the maximum Seidel energy. Our findings surpass existing general Seidel matrix energy limits and provide specific upper bounds for regular sequence graphs with degrees $d \geq 3$. We also examine the relationship between Seidel and Laplacian energies, and demonstrate that the Seidel and Laplacian energies are equivalent for regular sequence graphs with degree 3. This equivalence surpasses existing general matrix eigenvalue problems. Our methods include analyzing the Seidel matrix of a dihedral graph and linking it to the characteristic polynomial of the graph's vertex maps, which we express as $n^{r-1}$, where $n$ is the graph's order and $r$ is its degree. We also generalize the results to sequence graphs of order $n=2k+1$ for odd degrees and directly calculate the Seidel energy for the dihedral graph $\CQ_3$. We also investigate how the Seidel energy changes when the graph's vertex degrees change. This involves introducing a new concept: the Seidel $k$-energy, which calculates the Seidel energy for a submatrix of the Seidel matrix with the lowest $k$ diagonal entries. In our investigation, we extend optimal control issues governed by stochastic differential equations to multi-agent scenarios, where a large number of agents behave similarly and are influenced by a fractional Gaussian motion. This leads to a mean-field problem, which we resolve through two main steps. Firstly, we establish the existence of a solution to the related Hamiltonian System of Mean-Field Type. Subsequently, we demonstrate that this solution coincides with the optimal control outcome. To achieve this, we utilize the approach of Tykhonov regularization and introduce a compactness method. Ultimately, we prove that the resulting solution allows us to determine an optimal control strategy for a large number of agents. This work extends the principles of mean-field types of equations and optimal control, as first explored in [8, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19], to stochastic contexts, specifically within the frameworks of fractional Gaussian motion and Cauchy distributions, as well as stochastic differential equations and stochastic differential algebraic equations. Our study is closely related to applications in medicine and industry, as illustrated by the examples provided. Moreover, the research demonstrates that well-designed vehicle relays can enhance network coverage and reach farther distances. The outcomes of this study can be applied to other diverse networks, such as ad-hoc networks, and provide valuable insights for practitioners and researchers. The extensive collection of articles on Wikipedia constitutes a significant resource, yet its reliability cannot be guaranteed. This research aims to identify articles requiring improvement by analyzing the behavior of volunteers who edit them, as indicated by their contributions. Our analysis reveals that articles containing misinformation or of poor quality tend to lack robust references, exhibiting difficulty in being updated or modified. We observed editing patterns to develop an algorithm that accurately predicts articles requiring reference verification and those classified as low-quality candidates. This algorithm demonstrates exceptional accuracy in predicting unverified articles and a solid overall performance in predicting low-quality articles. Furthermore, the algorithm demonstrates a notable improvement in predicting low-quality articles when compared to existing methods. We have made our data available to the community, consisting of labeled articles and categories based on editing patterns, referred to as "EditTag". This dataset can facilitate the development of more sophisticated machine learning models and provide a valuable framework for detecting and correcting articles requiring improvement. Finally, we propose an automated system capable of identifying articles requiring improvement, with the goal of facilitating their correction by assigning tasks to volunteers based on their skills and article categories, thereby enhancing the collaborative process on Wikipedia. This initiative has the potential to be scaled up and adapted for other knowledge bases, such as Wiktionary and Knowledge Graphs. Current state-of-the-art multi-agent learning algorithms rely on extensive specialist demonstrations for each new task, which is impractical given the sheer number of possible objectives in many scenarios. Our proposed method, CoOL, enables two agents to learn a new cooperative task through observation of each other's interactions, without requiring any demonstrations specific to that task. By applying this approach to various cooperative games, such as the light-tunnel problem and the complex RoboThor platform, we have successfully induced up to 90% effective strategies in as few as 30 minutes of autonomous training. Unlike existing multi-agent learning methods, CoOL allows agents to generalize their skills across a range of unrelated objectives, which we have experimentally verified in multiple settings. Our proposed method encompasses two core components: the extraction of general task features from observed interactions, and the incorporation of these features into the agents' policy. By applying our method, agents can quickly learn to work together on tasks they have never encountered before, using only their prior experiences as a basis for generalization. We have publicly released the code for our method, as well as accompanying documentation, at https://github.com/steveninman/Cool/blob/master/Cool.ipynb. Our results demonstrate that Co-Observation without specialist Demonstration (CoOL) yields superior outcomes and faster training times than multiple alternative methods, while also promoting diversity in the strategies employed by the agents. This effectively enables the induction of cooperative policies on the fly, tailored to a wide range of objectives, and we have experimentally verified this effect in both controlled experiments and real-world applications. In particular, we have found that Co-Observation without specialist Demonstration (CoOL) produces up to 25% better outcomes and up to 2x faster training times than the next best alternative method, while also promoting diversity in the strategies employed by the agents. Our proposed method has numerous potential practical applications, and we have illustrated two examples in the text below, as well as in supplementary materials available online at https://steveninman.github.io/publications/Cool. Research on Polarization Alternating Coding (PAC) codes, a versatile coding technology, has been actively underway. Theoretical studies of PAC codes' performance have indicated they can approach the capacity of a communication channel, known as the polarization threshold, in the long term. In practice, measuring this performance and accurately decoding coded data becomes challenging due to the code's complex structure. A method developed in this research accurately calculates the polarization of channels when encoding is terminated, allowing for efficient decoding of received data. The proposed scheme's performance approaches that of optimal methods, while offering reduced computational complexity. Experimental results have shown the proposed algorithm to be resilient to varying conditions of channel quality and provides strong error protection. Its computational overhead is minimal, making it suitable for long-term applications. The research also provides a detailed analysis of the computational costs involved. The authors claim their work delivers the fastest known solution for decoding PAC codes, outperforming currently available algorithms by a significant margin. The study also showcases PAC codes' capabilities in 5G New Radio scenarios and highlights the decoding's simplicity, enabling direct implementation on the UCA and FUCA without the need for external libraries. The authors have further mitigated latency by partitioning the decoding process and using parallel processing. The proposed solutions have been validated using real-world scenarios, including simulations on SDA and ZCU204 boards, where the authors successfully implemented the decoder manually on the ZCU204 using VHDL, without any library involvement, and achieved up to 13.52X faster performance compared to the baseline implementation. The researchers have made their source code available on GitHub. The study has further explored and addressed various challenges in computing the transition probabilities of finite state machines necessary for PAC codes. The authors have derived a general approach applicable to multiple channels and provided a unified framework for calculating these probabilities, enabling accurate polarization measurements. The study has also derived a novel upper bound for polarization and established a direct relationship between transition probabilities and the critical threshold of the channel. The authors have further shown that analyzing channel symmetry suffices for determining polarization, greatly simplifying the computational load. The study has also proposed a new metric, the generalized polarization, and linked it to the critical threshold, enabling efficient estimation of the threshold from generalized polarization values. The authors have further developed an online decoder based on the generalized polarization metric, enabling accurate decoding of received data at any decoding depth. The study has also applied PAC codes to a 5G NR scenario, demonstrating their capability to approach the capacity of the channel and providing strong error protection with minimal computational overhead.

Specifically, this paper focuses on a model where treatment given to a subject affects not only themselves but also their K nearest neighbors. Our goal is to detect cases where the treatment given to these neighboring subjects is disrupted. By building on existing disruptions of continuous treatments, we develop a new concept - treatment discontinuity - for categorical treatments. particular, we show that under certain assumptions, the average treatment given to neighboring subjects can be distinct from their treated subject's choice without requiring any additional assumptions. Furthermore, we establish conditions under which a treated subject's most preferred choice is that which is given to their neighbors. Additionally, the possibility of neutrino-driven explosions triggered by Dark Matter annihilations is explored. Our analysis accounts for the detailed internal structure of Neutron Stars, including their surface composition, as well as the influence of nucleon-mediated Dark Matter interactions on neutrino emissions. Our results indicate that neutrino emissions from Dark Matter annihilations within Neutron Stars can be significantly intensified by non-pseudoscalar-mediated processes, particularly in regions near the star's surface. Consequently, neutrino emissions from Dark Matter annihilations may not make a supernova visible beyond a few kiloparsecs. However, the total neutrino energy may remain within the range that could potentially drive a supernova explosion. The influence of non-pseudoscalar-mediated Dark Matter interactions on neutrino emissions diminishes in dense regions of the star's core, where pseudoscalar-mediated processes dominate. As a result, neutrino emissions from Dark Matter annihilations within the core may be more effectively suppressed. Nevertheless, neutrino emissions from Dark Matter annihilations within the core remain a significant contributor to the total neutrino energy, as the core accounts for the majority of the star's volume. Therefore, while surface emissions may determine visibility and potential explosion, core processes remain pivotal in determining the total neutrino energy. The combination of our neutrino emission calculations from Dark Matter annihilations and existing supernova simulations may provide further insight into whether a supernova from Dark Matter annihilations could be distinguishable from a natural supernova explosion. Moreover, our analysis may offer constraints on the cross-section and mass of Dark Matter within a certain range by comparing the neutrino emissions from Dark Matter annihilations within Neutron Stars to a natural supernova. These findings contradict a previous prediction that the stabilizer rank of magic states must increase exponentially with the number of qubits. Our method is then extended to study magic states in higher dimensions, and we discover that the associated magic constants grow polynomially with the number of degrees of freedom. This result is surprising, given a previous demonstration that magic states in continuous Hilbert spaces have exponentially large stabilizer rank. Our work is supported by numerical evidence and influenced by a related finding that the resource distillation efficiency of quantum circuits, when described using a stabilizer framework, cannot exceed the square of a constant, typically set at one, unless additional resources are involved. It is hypothesized that this constant is actually a complex number with a modulus of at most $\sqrt{2}$, obtained from a specific family of states and their associated magic constants. This distillation efficiency perspective on the stabilizer rank approach is expected to be equivalent to a more traditional, circuit-based formulation of the problem. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the association of magic states with positive-norm stabilizer tensors, a property we refer to as "positivity," is not an essential aspect of their quantum nature, an interpretation that can be understood through the previously mentioned distinction between the stabilizer rank and a related quantity called the quasistabilizer rank. Our analysis starts from an observation that the positivity of magic states must decrease as their distance from the classical state increases, a scenario in which they are encoded within a specific family of quantum circuits. Feynman integrals are broken down into simpler components, called primitives, which have the same physical meaning as the original integrals. There are several methods to calculate these primitives, including entropy-based methods, temperature transformations, and causal representations. Despite being mathematically equivalent, these representations have different numerical properties, making some more suitable for certain applications. In our study, we examined the numerical value of 2-loop Feynman integrals essential for precision calculations in particle physics, specifically in the Delta phase-shift and the tau-lepton mass. Our analysis compares various representations of these integrals, highlighting their differences and showing that causal representations are generally more accurate than entropy-based methods, often requiring fewer calculations and with less numerical uncertainty. Furthermore, we found that temperature transformations can lead to negative results, which are physically infeasible, highlighting the benefits of causal representations for stable and physically meaningful outcomes. Our work also identified potential issues with entropy-based methods for certain integral types and demonstrated the effectiveness of an optimization technique to enhance numerical stability, resulting in a highly customized code for the Z boson mass calculation that showcases the superiority of causal representations in numerical evaluations. Additionally, we developed a new, customizable code based on causal representations for mass calculations in the Standard Model and its extensions, showcasing its efficiency and accuracy. Our study paves the way for a new, user-friendly software package to facilitate precise mass calculations in particle physics. All numerical data and code have been made publicly available to facilitate further research. In the future, we plan to expand our research to include more complex Feynman integrals, such as those involving external momentum dependencies, to further contribute to precision calculations in particle physics. The occurrence of non-Gaussian statistical patterns in an ensemble of laser-cooled particles has been theoretically determined for cases involving both conservative and dissipative optical lattices. A specific analysis was conducted on the probability distribution and variance of particles trapped in a two-color dissipative optical lattice, showing an increase in non-Gaussian behavior with lower particle densities and a corresponding divergence from the Gaussian distribution at very low densities, characterized by a long tail. In contrast, particles trapped in a conservative optical lattice displayed a statistical behavior more akin to a Gaussian distribution, albeit with a long, narrow tail. Measurements of the particle number and variances in an ensemble of particles trapped in both conservative and dissipative optical lattices verified that the presence of losses significantly alters the underlying statistical properties of the particles. It was further demonstrated that while both scenarios exhibit analogous behavior at low particle densities, the variances associated with particles trapped in a conservative optical lattice grow slowly with density, whereas those associated with particles trapped in a two-color dissipative optical lattice grow rapidly with density and are instead primarily determined by a dissipation-driven critical variances. In addition to these findings, predictions for the probability distribution and variance of particles trapped in a one-color dissipative optical lattice were generated using the solution for a two-color lattice. These theoretical predictions were validated against experimental results, showing close agreement between theory and experiment. These results provide the foundation for understanding Boillard and Bachelart's non-Gaussian behavior and extend their models to lower particle densities, effectively bridging the gap between their inelastic optical lattice model and the Hansen-Redfield model for laser-cooled particles. Moreover, these findings potentially enable the conversion of a conservative optical lattice, used to cool particles, into an innovative tool for generating non-Gaussian states of atoms. This novel approach could enable researchers to access previously inaccessible states of matter, thereby expanding our understanding of condensed matter physics. Lastly, these results also raise fundamental questions regarding the fluctuation-dissipation theorem and the Boltzmann equation, particularly at low particle densities where the presence of dissipation significantly alters the underlying statistical behavior of the particles. This study effectively merges the languages of quantum field theory and condensed matter physics, demonstrating a deeper connection between these disciplines. Finally, these results indicate that the principles governing quantum statistics remain relevant at very low particle densities, even in the presence of significant losses. This study provides theoretical and empirical evidence that quantum statistics remains relevant down to approximately ten particle densities.
