As marine robots navigate through dynamic ocean environments, their sensors' signals undergo significant changes over time. Current state estimation methods often fail to account for these temporal variations, leading to inaccurate predictions and models. In this research, we address this challenge by developing a novel sparse Gaussian process framework for modeling the evolution of data over time. This framework leverages sparse Gaussian processes to learn the patterns underlying signal changes, providing a more accurate and generalizable model. As a result, the proposed method outperforms traditional sparsification techniques, achieving better prediction and modeling outcomes, along with reduced computational and memory costs. Its effectiveness is demonstrated in a marine robot navigation application, where the algorithm successfully models the drift and fluctuation of acoustic and inertial sensor signals, allowing for accurate state estimation and modeling. Furthermore, the method is versatile and can be applied to other applications involving signal evolution, such as medical imaging and speech recognition. The code for the proposed method is available at https://github.com/whs815/kernels. Experimental data can be found at https://doi.org/10.6086/M2E15. In addition, a video showcasing the method's capabilities can be accessed at https://youtu.be/6h8h8xk7e4U. (Under review at IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters.)

Recent breakthroughs in AI have propelled the study of predicting relationships in temporal networks even further. These advanced models now enable the prediction of unobserved relationships in extensive datasets, significantly contributing to our comprehension of real-world events. Nonetheless, a persistent issue with these models remains their reliance on extensive, high-quality training data, often difficult and time-consuming to acquire, especially for newly emerging domains or individual entities within a dataset. To overcome this limitation, we propose an innovative approach that leverages existing knowledge to supplement limited and imperfect human observations, effectively bridging the gap between data scarcity and the need for accurate relationship predictions. This technique involves a straightforward strategy to determine the most likely unobserved relationships in a temporal network, yielding promising results, according to our experiments. These findings demonstrate that a substantial portion of unobserved relationships in a temporal network can be accurately predicted using established knowledge, even when a model is trained on a small, randomly selected subset of observations from that network. Additionally, our results indicate that the predictive capability of this strategy extends to newly emerging entities, where a significant percentage of their unobserved relationships can be accurately forecasted. Finally, our experiments also reveal that the application of this approach on a medical dataset enables the accurate forecasting of unobserved relationships for previously unrecorded diseases and their typically fixed duration of existence. These outcomes validate our hypothesis and demonstrate the potential of this technique to enable relationship forecasting even in data-scarce domains and beyond. You can find the code for our approach at https://github.com/asharif77/ForeCast. A short video summarizing our work is available at https://youtu.be/6h4bB1kUO7U. Additional information can be accessed via our website at https://forecast.ai.

Two infinite graph homomorphisms are equivalent if they can be transformed into each other through a series of elementary row operations. This equivalence is significant in C*-algebra studies, particularly in relating different infinite path algebras. However, this equivalence was only formally defined for directed graphs that have a finite source and a finite path, limiting its application. Recent research extends this notion to all row-finite directed graphs, demonstrating that its definition is consistent with existing criteria for such graphs. Additionally, this new definition meets the requirements for a valid equivalence relation, enabling the characterization of its reflexive and transitive components, as well as its relationship with the Morita equivalence in C*-algebras. The success of machine learning (ML) depends on vast amounts of data, which must be collected, prepared, and fed into ML systems to deliver accurate results. However, the data transformation process can be marred by issues such as corrupted or missing data, leading to model inaccuracies and poor performance. To rectify these problems, data engineers employ troubleshooting techniques, but these methods typically only focus on either data quality or model outcomes. In response, we introduce a new approach that combines the strengths of both strategies by determining which data to use for model training. We develop an innovative metric, the Shapley significance, to gauge the importance of individual data points for model accuracy. Our proposed method enables data quality to influence model training directly, allowing us to pinpoint problematic data and prevent model contamination. Experimental results on real-world datasets from different domains (astronomy and medicine) showcase the effectiveness of our approach in identifying irrelevant data and improving model performance, outperforming existing end-to-end ML workflows and data quality techniques. Furthermore, Shapley significance-enabled ML models exhibit enhanced robustness and accuracy in comparison to their conventional counterparts. The code for our approach is openly sourced on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/ParadiseResearchGroup/Data-Trouble-Shapley-Significance. We plan to expand on this work in the future by integrating our approach with other ML techniques from the literature. This study investigates how pressure affects the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn, a material that exhibits unique electronic properties due to Möbius strip frustration and pyrochlore skin effect. At ambient pressure, Mn$_3$Sn displays an in-plane Hall effect, but a critical pressure of 1.55 GPa induces a Hall effect along the axis, linked to a structural transformation that leads to a  quantized Hall effect above 20 K. Our computational analysis reveals that this phenomenon arises from a pressure-driven trimerization effect in Mn$_3$Sn, substantiated by structural and electronic property calculations. By modeling an external pressure of 4.69 GPa, our findings demonstrate that Trimerization plays a key role in regulating the anomalous Hall coefficient of Mn$_3$Sn, ultimately confirming that this material exhibits a quantized Hall effect within a broad temperature range of 8-220 K. As a result, Mn$_3$Sn offers an appealing starting point for realizing super-Quantum Hall effects at macroscopic scales. Additionally, its zero-net-magnetization structure makes it an ideal candidate for applications involving spin-orbit-tronics. We predict that Mn$_3$Sn's Hall effect can be modulated through temperature, and that this behavior is further regulated by Sn's p-d hybridization, ultimately giving rise to an in-plane Hall effect below 20 K and an axial Hall effect above this threshold. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of how pressure and Trimerization can regulate the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn. Furthermore, computational analysis of nearest-neighbor Mn interactions, as well as magnetic moments in Mn, reveals that Trimerization leads to a stabilization of antiferromagnetic order in this material. Our findings confirm that Mn interactions are strongly regulated by pressure-driven Trimerization, ultimately giving rise to unique electronic properties in Mn$_3$Sn. As an added benefit, our study provides a comprehensive understanding of how Trimerization regulates magnetic interactions at the atomic scale, offering a comprehensive explanation for the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn. Ultimately, this material offers an appealing starting point for exploring the behavior of ferromagnets, antiferromagnets, and ferri-magnets within a single phase. As such, Mn$_3$Sn provides an ideal candidate for spintronics applications and spin-orbit-tronics, and our study provides a comprehensive understanding of how Trimerization and pressure can regulate the Hall effect in this material

This study explores a Steklov-Robin type eigenvalue problem associated with the Laplace operator in a rectangle with a finite number of holes. The operator acts on a function f(x,y) with Dirichlet boundary conditions on the exterior boundaries and a Steklov-Robin boundary condition on the interior boundaries. The interior boundaries are assumed to be perfectly conducting. Unlike the standard Steklov problem, which only considers perfectly conducting or perfectly insulating boundaries, this problem incorporates a combination of these scenarios. The primary focus is on deriving asymptotic approximations of the eigenvalues by analyzing the exterior boundary condition and relating it to a singular perturbation problem. These approximations are accurate to the second order. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that these approximations accurately represent the large eigenvalue index. To confirm these findings, comparisons are made with a related interior Steklov problem and the results from approximating the eigenvalues through the asymptotic analysis are validated by means of a numerical study based on the first 20 eigenvalues of the problem. The study also provides a theoretical justification for the method used to approximate the eigenvalues in a related problem. Specifically, it justifies the use of specific functionals in a variational approach to determine the eigenvalues in a related problem. The approaches used to determine the eigenvalues in this problem and its variants are essentially variational in nature. The order of the eigenvalues is confirmed by means of a min-max principle that generalizes to various scenarios. The methods used to analyze this problem can be applied more broadly to domains with various types of geometric scaling. The analysis in this problem could also be applied to study the behavior of functions near their singularities. The problem can be generalized to act on different functions and with various operators acting on the Laplace and Steklov-Robin problems in various domains with inclusions. The analysis in this problem also provides a framework for studying the homogenization of periodic problems and various other problems and their related variants. The problem can also be used to study the spectral quantization of classical chaos and various other problems and their related variants. The methods used to analyze this and related problems could also be applied to study the Steklov problem in domains with conic inclusions and various other problems and their related variants. The problem can also be used to extend the classical Steklov problem to various domains with inclusions and singularities. Improving image quality using non-destructive enhancement techniques is a crucial task. Existing state-of-the-art methods primarily focus on enhancing images guided by a single reference, overlooking the inherent connections within the data. To address this, we propose Guided Hypergraph Restoration (GHR), a novel framework that leverages guided image restoration to reveal hidden details in the data while considering the complex interrelationships among the inputs. Through extensive experimentation on various applications such as denoising, deblocking, and decompression, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, which outperforms existing methods significantly, especially in the case of challenging low-quality inputs. To facilitate reproducibility, our code and datasets can be accessed at https://github.com/PCBao/GHR. GHR has been approved for publication in the Journal of Visual Communication and Image Representation, with the approval number JVCIR20220073.

To expand our understanding of how radiologists analyze chest X-rays, we created detailed annotations on over 200,000 X-rays by recreating them as 3D volumes from CT scans and having human annotators mark key features.  We also developed new, detailed annotations for lung conditions, drawing from publicly available data.  We found that our custom annotations allow machines to learn and perform better than standard image classification.  Ultimately, we hope these resources will help radiologists better understand how human radiologists make diagnoses and inform the development of more effective medical image analysis systems.  Our data is available at https://radiology.ucsd.edu/cxr-projections/ for use by the research community.

We have generalized this formula to tight contact frameworks, which are contact structures on the configurations of a polynomial knot or link in 3D space. The characteristic of a tight contact framework is calculated as the sum of norms (plus 2) of the matrix representing the framework's regular compact components. The norm in question is known as the Thurston norm. Consequently, all values of the Euler characteristic for a framework that is tight and in contact are less than or equal to its topological invariant. Furthermore, if a framework that is in contact and tight consists solely of a knot whose equation is polynomial, then its lowest possible value of the Euler characteristic that is tight and in contact is 1. In this case, we can also determine the number (counting multiplicities) of the value 1 that is tight and in contact for the framework: it is equal to the number (counting multiplicities) of the lowest regular value of the framework's regular level sets. Lastly, we have established that there are an infinite number of tight contact frameworks that are unique. Similarly, there are an infinite number of tight contact frameworks that are unique and in contact. Additionally, there are an infinite number of tight contact frameworks that are unique, in contact, and in motion. They are all unique. In microcavity lasers, carefully aligned reflective surfaces can generate unidirectional electromagnetic releases. A statistical analysis, specifically the calculation of the von Neumann entropy for photon fields, is employed to investigate the bilateral discharges and assess their directional output. A comparison between the linear and nonlinear responses to these investigations is made. Furthermore, a method for quantifying anisotropic effects is developed, utilizing the entropy and its derivative, and is applied to scenarios involving square and circular microcavity designs. A semi-analytical approach, combining approximate anisotropy quantification with semi-classical laser theory, yields intuitive physical results and accurately forecasts low-power venture behaviors. An interesting phenomenon is noted, where entropy displays hysteresis under varying coupling strength, indicating a fundamental balance between the two directional releases. This study provides valuable insights into understanding and identifying anisotropic electromagnetic releases in microcavity lasers through entropy analysis. It also paves the way for the application of entropy in assessing directional outputs in other microphotonics systems. It is anticipated that this research will contribute to the development of innovative, highly efficient unidirectional microphotonics technologies. Such technologies could potentially utilize entropy-based approaches for precise control of electromagnetic releases at the microscale. Our analysis of digital currencies like Bitcoin highlights the challenges they face in maintaining their underlying exchange mechanisms. These challenges arise from the nature of their creators, the miners, who act as intermediaries in transactions. To resolve this, we propose a new approach, called cost consistency, that ensures a fair exchange process among all parties involved. This proposal forms the foundation of a theoretical model, called CCX, for digital currency design. Furthermore, we have examined the feasibility of integrating cost consistency into existing blockchain technology by investigating a modified version of the Bitcoin exchange process. This investigation leads to a polynomial-time algorithm for solving the resulting integer programming problem. Ultimately, our findings demonstrate that incorporating cost consistency can yield more efficient transaction outcomes. Additionally, we have explored key aspects of our exchange model, such as its compatibility with diverse payment protocols and the potential for strategic behavior in transactions. Our subsequent study will delve into transaction negotiations, examining how participants can agree on terms that maximize their individual welfare. This research will likely have further implications for understanding the economics of digital currencies. Lastly, our analysis shows that transaction costs can be substantial in the Bitcoin network, supporting our concept of cost consistency and highlighting its potential for improving the transaction experience. This finding is likely to extend to other digital currencies as well. To validate our ideas, we conducted an in-depth survey among Bitcoin users, asking them about their perceptions of transaction costs and the importance of a fair exchange process. Our results indicate that a significant majority of respondents agree on the importance of transaction fees as a means for miners to compensate for their work. This discovery provides valuable insights for further research into the economics of digital currencies. This paper is organized as follows. In Section 1, we provide an in-depth examination of our exchange model, CCX, along with its underlying principles. In Section 2, we discuss the algorithm for solving the integer programming problem resulting from our exchange model. In Section 3, we investigate the feasibility of incorporating cost consistency into existing blockchain technology by modifying the Bitcoin exchange process. In Section 4, we explore key aspects of our exchange model, CCX, and its underlying payment protocols. In Section 5, we report on our survey among Bitcoin users regarding transaction costs and the fairness of the exchange process. In Section 6, we analyze the efficiency of transaction outcomes. In Section 7, we discuss strategic transaction negotiations. In Section 8, we conclude our research and outline the content of our companion paper. In Appendix 1, we provide a detailed proof of the polynomial-time complexity of our transaction outcome

Election manipulation through the alteration of voting districts constitutes a long-standing issue in the United States. To address this, we propose an innovative method to measure unfair electoral divisions by applying simulated tempering to a model representing district formation. This method, quantified through Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulations, yields a clear and easily interpretable measure of fairness. We demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods for detecting unfair electoral divisions. Furthermore, we highlight that, similar to statistical models, political gerrymandering analysis benefits significantly from incorporating additional information, such as party affiliations, to enhance accuracy. Our technique is versatile and can be applied to different forms of unfair division without relying on prior knowledge. As a result, we hope that our work will inspire researchers to utilize their skills in addressing this critical societal problem. The code for our methods is freely accessible on our website at https://forthestate.org/contact.

Textile images exhibit unique characteristics of low color value, sparse pixels, and irregularities due to the inherent properties of the fabric material, resulting in distorted or flawed images that must be identified and corrected.  Removing flaws from these images is crucial for evaluating a fabric's quality and ensuring consistency in production.  Currently, there is no universal flaw removal method suitable for all types of textile images.  This paper proposes an innovative approach to flaw identification and removal for textile images featuring unique patterns, utilizing the generalized extension of the Generalized HOG operator and low-rank matrix decomposition.  The proposed method involves several key contributions:  First, we apply the GHOG operator to convert textured regions into a more meaningful, low-dimensional feature space.  Next, we seek minimal pixels with the highest contribution to image distortion, seeking the lowest-rank solution through matrix decomposition.  Finally, the corrected image is obtained by subtracting the flaw map from the original textile image.  Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in flaw removal for various textile images, displaying improved color, sparse pixel, and rank values.  Additionally, we have released the textile_flaw_correction toolbox, providing a range of useful tools for textile flaw correction.  This toolbox can be accessed via http://www.iaec.edu.cn/indexy.html, under the category of image processing. To succeed in visual navigation with Reinforcement Learning, a agent must effectively utilize visual cues from camera feeds to build a map of its surroundings. This goal is challenging due to intermittent reinforcement from the environment, mapless navigation, and the reliance on low-resolution visual inputs. Current state-of-the-art models, such as VCN and VRN, leverage multi-camera views and attentional image encoding to achieve impressive performance. However, their mapless navigation capabilities are restricted to indoor settings and are susceptible to low-reward paths and brittle generalization. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a new model, Navigation from Few Views (NFFV), which exploits a novel data-driven regularization technique to enhance navigation efficiency and robustness. This method employs a forward predictive model that estimates the agent's future states and incorporates a regularization term that enforces agreement between the agent's current map and future observations. Experimental results demonstrate the agent's ability to navigate diverse indoor and outdoor settings using only a few camera views, surpassing existing models and achieving state-of-the-art performance with regularization. A demonstration video is available at https://youtu.be/6h4bY7b1G7g. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/AAronR/NFFV.adas.ao.20.

Our research reveals that supermassive black holes experiencing repeated outbursts over cosmic time must have had their masses significantly diminished in the past in order to accommodate the existing diversity of their masses today, given the rapid evolution of the universe. This conclusion arises from the product relationship between Bondi mass and time in the black hole's vicinity, as specified by the self-similar inner accretion model. However, such a history of massive black hole downsizing is at odds with our current understanding of black hole growth, as it implies an unfeasibly high rate of mass loss per unit area. To resolve this discrepancy, we propose that a feedback mechanism must be in effect, slowing the black hole's mass accumulation and thus extending the time needed for them to reach their present masses. Alternatively, our findings may simply reflect a shortcoming in the self-similar accretion model's ability to accurately capture the complex dynamics of black hole accretion and mergers on long cosmic timescales. Conversely, this discrepancy could also provide evidence for a feedback mechanism that slows the black hole's mass accumulation, or it could require a reevaluation of our current understanding of black hole accretion and mergers over long cosmic timescales. Moreover, our research suggests that a black hole's growth is likely to be turbulent and unpredictable over long cosmic timescales, even in a scenario where the black hole continuously accretes uniformly from its surrounding gas. Furthermore, we develop a categorical framework that characterizes quadrics based on the properties of the mapping's kernel and 2-form. This approach enables the description of singularities through Morita equivalence for all quadrics. Additionally, we define a novel intrinsic 2-form on the non-commutative projective space, which describes the geometric relationships between line bundles, 1-forms, and 2-forms. Text-based games provide a challenging platform to assess virtual agents in simulating human-like conversation and problem-solving abilities. These games' complexity stems from their open-ended nature, making it difficult for agents to learn from short episodes. To overcome this issue, researchers typically use predefined heuristics or agent-specific models tailored to each game, but these are not transferable to other games. To create a more universal testing platform, we developed TextWorldExpress, an emulated version of text-based games, allowing for large-scale synthetic training. By leveraging an optimized data structure and vectorized operations, we achieved a remarkable speed upgrade of one million, enabling extensive training on a single GPU. We successfully trained a basic agent using deep reinforcement learning on a dataset of 125 billion transitions. These agents can now be directly applied to a wide range of text-based games without any further fine-tuning, demonstrating a significant improvement in solving these games. The open-source TextWorldExpress framework empowers researchers to conduct large-scale synthetic training, expands the scope of text-based games, and promotes the development of more sophisticated agents. Furthermore, it offers pre-trained models that can solve a variety of challenging text-based games, paving the way for novel applications in natural language processing. These models not only outperform existing agents but also serve as a common language model, facilitating cross-training and knowledge-sharing between different games. To accelerate research, we launched the TextWorldExpress Hall of Fame, showcasing the top-performing models, which have demonstrated impressive results in solving a range of text-based games. To obtain our source code, datasets, and pre-trained models, visit our website at https://textworldexpr.github.io/. We invite researchers to join the TextWorldExpress community and contribute to the development of more advanced text-based game solutions. Keywords: text-based games, reinforcement learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, TextWorldExpress, emulated games, synthetic training.

When a robot interacts with a human, its interactive manipulability realm defines the area in space where stable interaction is achieved by adjusting the robot's joint angles. This study proposes a novel approach to align the robot's manipulability realm with that of a person. This alignment is critical to the development of safe human-robot collaboration and is the focus of our research. Our method considers the complex, nonlinear relationships between the robot's joint angles and its position in 3D space, taking into account the inherent singularity points that make this calculation challenging. To achieve this, we leverage the properties of smooth manifolds to create a framework for comparing the robot's manipulability realm with human data. Once the robot's manipulability realm is established, our implementation of the Iterative Closest Point algorithm allows us to project human poses onto the suitable surface, effectively aligning the robot and human manipulability realms. Through real-world experiments using a Universal Robot, we demonstrate that this alignment can be achieved with precision, even in the presence of complex obstacles. Our findings show that the robot's manipulability realm is robustly determined and can be reliably aligned with human data, providing a safe and stable foundation for human-robot collaboration. In the real world, objects often rotate around various axes, and their owners may not even intend to do so. We propose a novel, unsupervised method to learn an object's 3D position from video footage, without requiring any specific training. Our approach relies on a unique rotation pipeline that identifies objects spinning around any axis, allowing it to track their movement in both the object's and the camera's coordinate system. By combining these results with optical flow information, we estimate the 3D position of the object, even when the camera doesn't directly point at it. Our method outperforms other 3D learning techniques, including those that use depth information, demonstrating substantial accuracy across diverse datasets, including unsupervised and traditional benchmark datasets. Our code is publicly available.

The rapid development of a COVID-19 vaccine offers a chance to regain societal normalcy, yet widespread skepticism about its efficacy persists, fueled in part by misinformation circulating online. The dissemination of false information about vaccines through social media platforms poses a significant threat, prompting concerns about consumer safety. Researchers propose an innovative task that automates the detection of vaccine-related misinformation in Twitter conversations and identifies the acceptance or rejection of such misinformation. A proposed approach, using long short memory networks, is proposed to classify the stance towards vaccination on a scale of absolute disagreement to absolute agreement. An experiment was conducted with 1,536 human annotators who labeled data for a model trained by Google, indicating that the model achieved 57% F1 score without further refinement. Additionally, an in-depth case study was performed to analyze model outputs and provide contextual insights into the detection of vaccine-related misinformation in Twitter conversations. Moreover, the results showed the importance of considering dialogue when determining the stance towards vaccination, as opposed to simply evaluating individual tweets. Furthermore, the results showed that the model correctly predicted the stance towards vaccination in 69% of cases when trained on 3,600 professionally annotated data points, as opposed to 57% F1 score in the Twitter dataset. This study presents an innovative approach to generating synthetic speech using a non-statistical method, enabling the production of speech with varied lengths. Inspired by the median control strategy of intrinsic motivated image compression (IMIC), we developed a neural network called the median drive model (MDM). The MDM is comprised of two components: a length estimator and a variable-length sequence predictor. The length estimator identifies the target speech's median length by analyzing its fundamental frequency, then divides it into segments. The sequence predictor synthesizes speech in these segments using the median length as guidance. Our model can predict speech lengths accurately and generate synthetic speech with lengths different from that of the training data. The results demonstrate a significant enhancement in the synthesis of various length speech samples compared to a model without a length estimator. Furthermore, a comparison with a statistical model, a transformer-based sequence-to-sequence model, reveals the superiority of the MDM in predicting speech lengths and the quality of its synthetic speech. The effectiveness of the MDM is confirmed through listening tests, where a panel of human listeners preferred the synthetic speech produced by the MDM. The implementation details, including the length estimator's parameters and the model's coding efficiency, are also provided. Additionally, a demonstration of the MDM's ability to learn a general length estimation principle is presented. Our research not only introduces an innovative approach to synthetic speech of various lengths but also explores the thermodynamic principles underlying IMIC, a topic that requires further theoretical analysis. Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals how disease transmission rates and network characteristics, like clustering and dispersal, influence the outbreak. However, hypergraphs provide a more comprehensive framework for modeling these events, capturing interactions between multiple individuals in a single event. This study initiates the examination of epidemics on hypergraphs through the development of a new extinction threshold on these structures, derived from the hypergraph's spectral properties. This threshold measures the average transmission rate at which the epidemic can only spread infinitely versus extinguish. To calculate this critical value, we first determine the spectral boundaries of the hypergraph's Laplacian, then develop an approximate formula for its largest eigenvalue. This work also considers more complex scenarios, such as multiple infection events and the impact of stochasticity, before simulating these processes numerically. The results show that the predicted extinction threshold accurately predicts the critical transmission rate in many cases and serves as a suitable approximation in others. The associated code for these simulations is publicly accessible at https://github.com/agb2910/Extinction-Thresholds-on-Hypergraphs. The research was partially funded by EPSRC with project ID EP/T008802/1. This helps advance knowledge in both hypergraph Laplacian eigenvalues and the analysis of epidemics on more intricate network types, like hypergraphs, to model real events more accurately, such as the spread of COVID-19 in close-living communities. The research provides a theoretical foundation and a practical tool, the AGP3 algorithm, for determining the critical transmission rate in these situations. The study expands knowledge by applying this approach to more complex hypergraphs than previously studied and makes the associated code publicly available to replicate the results. A cutting-edge solution for multimodal classification is presented in the form of a flexible neural network architecture.  We've integrated the benefits of shared representations and modular, separately-trained models for complex feature analysis.  The latter approach mimics the K-fan method, while maintaining the ability to learn and process individual modalities independently.  The proposed system is a versatile extension of existing solutions, suitable for resolving a wide range of classification challenges.  Its fundamental configuration allows for the separation of modalities and their associated attributes, akin to the K-fan model.  Furthermore, we've refined this configuration by introducing a shared-representation module to harmonize the learned models and facilitate inter-modal integration.  We've also developed a dual-learning mechanism to enhance the separate training of modalities and their attribute models.  As a result, our Generalized K-fan framework (GKF) surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art solutions, as validated by extensive experiments on small, medium, and large datasets.  Specifically, our GKF outperforms alternative solutions by up to 3.7% in terms of accuracy, while reducing parameter complexity by up to 70%.  Consequently, our proposed method exhibits superior performance and efficiency across a range of real-world applications.  You can access the code at https://github.com/zhengyuchu4/GKF.git. This paper introduces McMini, a lightweight tool for verifying the correctness of multithreaded programs based on McBurney's work. McMini uses a configurable technique to evaluate the reachability of bad states in a program's execution. The tool is highly adjustable and can be tailored to fit various program models by selecting a suitable representation and underlying state machine. A key aspect of McMini is its ability to facilitate the comparison of different verification approaches, as demonstrated through the evaluation of two case studies. One case study explores the effects of machine-specific architecture on thread execution, while the second examines the impact of thread synchronization mechanisms. Both case studies highlight the advantages of McMini's flexibility in improving efficiency and reducing computation time. The source code for McMini is freely available on the GitLab repository located at: https://gitlab.com/mcmini/mcmini. Additionally, the McMini repository contains a range of configurable benchmarks, including McBurney's original benchmark suite and two new sets of benchmarks in x86 IR and C that were used in the case studies. The widespread use of social media has highlighted the significant issue of misinformation dissemination. In countries such as India, large-scale misinformation leading to mass fatalities has prompted policymakers to explore ways to curb its spread. One strategy, implemented by WhatsApp in India during the 2020 election period, involves limiting the forwarding capabilities of certain messages to five recipients. In this research, we investigate the effect of this policy in India by analyzing user behavior on the platform. Our study reveals that WhatsApp's measures led to a substantial 70% decline in forwarded messages. However, we also found that, contrary to the company's claims, the majority of these restricted messages were originally forwarded by a small group of prolific users. Furthermore, these users continued to engage freely in other chat groups. Our analysis suggests that WhatsApp's policy primarily shifted the dissemination of user-generated content, rather than significantly reducing the total amount shared. While the company's measures resulted in a notable reduction in forwarded messages, they did little to address the underlying behaviors of the most active forwarders. We introduce the Activation mechanism (Amech) to improve the performance of existing methods in detecting spoofing attacks. By analyzing the activation of neurons in a deep neural network, we found that certain neurons exhibit significant biases due to improper training, thus weakening the network's overall performance. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of Amech in enhancing the performance of deep neural networks on spoken identification spoofing countermeasures. Additionally, our method's generalizability was validated by applying it to multiple datasets. We also compared our method with alternative approaches aimed at optimizing neuron activation, such as regularization techniques. Bloom filters provide quick, memory-efficient approximations of set membership, but their design has limitations. In contrast, more advanced filters like Bloom and Cuckoo filters can be used in higher-level programming languages, despite their poor performance compared to other alternatives. A new class of filters, called xor filters, has been designed with the opposite priorities: they prioritize speed and adaptability to modern computing environments while sacrificing some accuracy. The trade-off involves inserting multiple elements into a hash table before adding them to the filter. We show that existing filters can be improved upon by introducing a new construction of exact filters, and we modify Bloom and Cuckoo filters to use hash tables, effectively creating xor filters. The resulting xor filters offer faster false positives and better scalability than their Bloom and Cuckoo filter counterparts. Moreover, they require less memory to achieve the same false positive rate, and they support modulated insertion of arbitrary data, making them more versatile. A key advantage of xor filters is their ability to be implemented efficiently in higher-level languages, and we provide benchmarks to support this claim. Ultimately, xor filters offer a simple and efficient solution to the approximate membership problem, and they can be easily adapted for both exact and probabilistic applications. The authors make their code available under an open-source license at https://github.com/constantin-f/cxorf. Additionally, a faster, more compact implementation of Bloom filters can be found at https://github.com/constantin-f/buf. Further information on the design of xor filters and related topics can be found at https://cfresearch.net. This paper reports on the findings from the 2022 Out-of-Lexicon Word Sense Disambiguation (OXL-WSD) competition. The competitive dataset comprises sentences containing unfamiliar words, and participants were tasked with identifying their correct meanings. A combination of support vector machines and string similarity features emerged as the top approach to conquer this unconventional WSD problem. The winning teams' models exhibit an average F1 score of 50.87 for the comprehensive task, with some models even achieving satisfactory results on the more restrictive baseline tasks. Deep learning model training faces significant obstacles due to the vast computational requirements, long training times, and extensive memory consumption of complex models. While model pruning has been shown to address these issues, current approaches often simplify the network architecture, lacking the original features. This paper presents ClickTrain, a novel end-to-end training framework that combines both effective model reduction and precise feature retention. The method involves representing subnets within the original model via binary indicators and optimizing these indicators through end-to-end training. The resulting models exhibit preserved accuracy and the benefits of reduced complexity, yielding superior performance and computational efficiency. The method is versatile, applicable to various pruning methods, and can be adapted for both quantitative and qualitative click training. The proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches on CNNS, ResNet-50, MobileNetV2, and DNNs, offering substantial runtime and memory resource improvements. Superquantum mechanics, an extension of quantum mechanics for spin-1/2 particles, lacks a established formalism.  Two distinct approaches have been proposed to address this issue: the superquantum mechanics of Yang and his colleagues, which incorporates extra symmetry, and a variant proposed by Witten, which ties into the moduli space of supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory.  This latter model is shown to mirror the expansion of cohomology from the Borel-Weil-Bott theorem.  Consequently, this model can translate physical properties into geometric properties of the moduli space, thereby facilitating the computation of quantities like superpairing correlation functions via the Jacobi form method.  Ultimately, this model is found to retain the fundamental characteristics of the superquantum mechanics of Yang and his colleagues.  Additionally, this formalism is demonstrated to have a analogous counterpart in superconformal field theory. This superfield formalism is found to be closely related to the moduli space formulation described herein.  Specifically, both methods share a common connection via the Lefschetz fixed-point formula. The conventional linear algebra and the basic probability theory are insufficient for analyzing complex, fluctuating networks.  These types of networks, characterized by in-degree, out-degree, and weight of edges, interact with nodes generating output based on feedback from incoming signals.  The stability of the system relies on the system's ability to regulate itself, limiting excessive variability.  We have developed a mathematical framework for studying this self-regulation and it is applicable across a wide range of network topologies.  By analytically calculating the average and the variance of the output signals, as well as the injected currents, we have mathematically defined the self-regulation mechanism.  We have further demonstrated the validity of our approach through numerical simulations of a neuronal network model.  The results show that as the out-degree of a neuron increases, its response becomes more stable, but also less responsive to external stimuli.  The out-degree also affects the responsiveness of other neurons in the network, leading to a decrease in their variability and making them more dependent on the primary neuron.  Similarly, increasing the weight of a neuron's edges results in a decrease in the corresponding variable and output, but also in a decrease in the injected currents and variability of other neurons.  These findings are independent of the network's initial conditions and are applicable across a broad range of complex network topologies.  The self-regulation mechanism we have defined provides a general framework for studying variability in complex networks and can be widely adopted for analyzing various types of complex systems.  Furthermore, our approach may also contribute to a better understanding of spontaneous neural activity in living organisms. The Riemann Hypothesis, a cornerstone of number theory for over a century, has eluded resolution despite significant efforts. This paper presents an alternative approach to prime number theory, one that assumes only the truth of a modified Riemann Hypothesis. Based on this assumption, this proof draws upon a specialized complex number theory result, known as the Prime Value Theorem. This proof yields a simplified demonstration of the modified Twin Prime Conjecture, as well as the infiniteness of prime numbers of every form $2a_n n^2 + 1$. Additionally, this framework allows for the derivation of a modified Goldbach Conjecture, which states that any natural number greater than $2$ can be expressed as the sum of two prime numbers. Finally, this framework is shown to imply the existence of an arithmetic progression comprising infinitely many prime numbers, given specific conditions. The Prime Value Theorem, in turn, is proved by integrating elements of the Selberg zeta function and the Riemann zeta function. The assumption of a modified Riemann Hypothesis is crucial in this integration. The zeta function's analytic continuation and the critical zeros of its logarithmic derivative, $\zeta'(.)$, are key outcomes derived from this proof, which in turn enable the derivation of the Prime Value Theorem. The utility of this new framework is demonstrated through several examples, including the verification of a modified Twin Prime Conjecture and the confirmation of an arithmetic progression comprising infinitely many prime numbers, both of which had already been previously established. The approach taken here offers potential avenues for further exploration and extension. Although previous research focused on constructing pessimistic off-policy dynamic treatment regimes, it is generally impractical due to its reliance on certain conditions in high-dimensional settings. We will also examine the properties of Yoneda squares in relation to duality types and explain how Yoneda triangles can be derived from 2-cfunctors in the presence of a matrix representing dualities. Additionally, the relationship between matrix dualities and Serre duality will be explored, and we will extend the concept of matrix dualities to categories of tilting modules, Koszul modules, and Gorenstein modules. The article will also discuss how matrix dualities can be utilized to compute invariants such as the Euler form, Koszul form, and Hochschild cohomology of a quotient algebra by a subalgebra. Several examples will be utilized to illustrate the concepts and demonstrate their practical applications. The article concludes by highlighting the avenues for future research in the field. The article aims to provide an accessible introduction to the subject for graduate students and young researchers, assuming a basic understanding of matrix dualities, Serre duality, and tilting theory. The article can be considered a didactic article with instructional content, providing an overview of the subject with explicit examples and straightforward proofs. Existence-absence data presents positive or negative observations on a large number of variables for a single subject. This type of data is commonly seen in fields such as ecology and microbiology. The primary challenge in analyzing this data is the handling of zeros, which are not necessarily absent entities. This research demonstrates how to apply the Kullback-Leibler clustering method to existing-absent data and compares its performance with other popular clustering approaches. Our evaluation included multiple datasets from ecology and microbiology to test the effectiveness of different methods in retaining the original data structure. The results showed that the Kullback-Leibler method outperformed other techniques in preserving the underlying structure of these datasets. Additionally, the integration of multidimensional scaling before applying the Kullback-Leibler method or a Gaussian-based approach did not significantly improve performance. However, our findings also revealed that these clustering methods struggle with existing-absent data that lacks clear underlying structures. A comprehensive software implementation is provided for these methods to ensure accessibility and reproducibility. A tutorial on using the software is also included to assist users in applying these methods to their own data. The software package known as clustexistabs is written in R and Python to address the analysis needs mentioned above. In computer vision, salient item identification focuses on pinpointing objects of supreme importance within an image or its three-dimensional depth projection. This paper introduces an innovative, integrated framework for detecting salient items in both RGB and RGB-D images. Our method seamlessly fuses visual information from RGB and depth maps to accurately identify the most critical objects. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of our framework, which surpasses existing benchmarks and effectively retains the original image details. To validate the efficacy of our method, a novel dataset containing 400 images, dubbed SIPI, is created and utilized. The SIPI dataset comprises 200 pairs of RGB images along with their corresponding depth projections, carefully annotated to guide state-of-the-art salient item detection algorithms and a proposed baseline. A comprehensive evaluation of these methods on the SIPI dataset reveals that our integrated framework consistently yields superior results. The proposed framework is made accessible on our website in the form of open-source code, enabling other researchers to build upon our work. A companion study also highlights the distinct advantages of salient item detection over more conventional salient object detection and semantic segmentation tasks. To facilitate reproducibility, our dataset, as well as the employed training and evaluation protocols, are freely available at the provided link. Moreover, a comprehensive analysis of our method's performance on additional 10 categories is provided, showcasing its versatility and effectiveness on a broader range of scenarios. The proposed framework is comprised of two interconnected components, a cross-modal fusion module and a coherent reconstruction module, which work in tandem to pinpoint salient items within an image or its depth projection. Our integrated framework leverages an innovative yet straightforward self-attention cross-modal fusion module that efficiently combines RGB and depth information to accurately identify salient items. A figure is considered palindromic if it reads the same when viewed from the top and bottom, and not palindromic otherwise. In this study, we examine ratios of palindromic to non-palindromic figures for various scenarios, and derive accurate mathematical descriptions for these ratios. Our analysis extends existing research on the enumeration of palindromic figures, as reported by Knuth, Sweet, and Larson. We particularly focus on the following scenarios: growing figures, growing figures with outside growth, figurate numbers, and triangular numbers. Our findings demonstrate that while the distribution of palindromic and non-palindromic numbers may initially appear random, it actually adheres to a precise, repeating pattern governed by a simple mathematical formula. This pattern is analogous to the distribution of palindromic and non-palindromic numbers in a random sequence. Our calculations are accurate enough to determine the palindromic ratio for any figurate number with a depth of at least 286, as well as the corresponding general term. Similarly, our calculations are precise enough to determine the palindromic ratio for triangular numbers with a depth of at least 533. Our research also uncovers a hidden, non-obvious mathematical connection between the general terms of the palindromic and antipalindromic sequences, which holds true in an abstract mathematical context known as a 'category'. This discovery is particularly significant because the underlying reason for this connection is unclear, and it may be related to a fundamental property of numbers or a statistical phenomenon. Ultimately, our findings resolve several previously acknowledged conjectures and pose new questions for further exploration. We also create and utilize two distinct computational tools - a type of mathematical algorithm - to aid in our calculations: the 'lattice triangle' generator and the 'triangular order' database. These tools not only facilitate our specific research but may also have a range of additional applications in mathematics. Our work, in turn, enables the exploration of previously unexamined problems using a methodical approach, thereby shedding new light on the underlying mathematics. Our novel mathematical algorithm - the 'palindromic rule' - can be utilized to determine whether any given number is palindromic or not, and it does so using a straightforward, easily computable formula. Computed tomography (CT) is a widely employed medical imaging technique that uses low-energy x-rays to create detailed cross-sectional images of the human body. In a CT scanner, x-rays of various energy levels are directed at a patient and the resulting attenuation coefficients are used to reconstruct images. However, manufacturing defects and multiple energy sources can complicate image quality, while detector noise further degrades the signals, and the biological body is composed of materials that change with time, such as tissues that absorb x-rays but do not emit them. To overcome these limitations, a non-convex optimization framework is proposed to simultaneously handle CT system imperfections, noise, and the time-varying decomposition of scanned materials into known components. The model is tested using synthetic and real data from a Geant4 simulation and a patient with an abdominal aneurysm, respectively. While the model demonstrates promising results for simultaneous reconstruction and material breakdown, it is limited by slow computational processing times that can exceed actual data collection times, indicating a need for further improvement. To mitigate this, a simplified and more efficient convex model is developed for optimal x-ray energy and material decomposition, which outperforms traditional iterative reconstruction methods but still falls short of the non-convex approach in image quality. The researchers suggest several future directions, including the incorporation of non-destructive material models and the extension of the framework to simultaneous back-projection and sensor denoising. Furthermore, the team plans to integrate the proposed framework into a scanner control system, allowing the scanner to collect data tailored to optimal solutions, effectively turning the process into a destructive materials testing system. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources remains a complex challenge due to the scarcity of labeled data, significant character variability, and a vast vocabulary. To overcome these limitations, we focus on single-shot data augmentation by capturing handwritten text along with its contextual description during the writing process, producing a composite dataset. This approach enables us to create a large quantity of data without relying on manual labels, thereby improving model performance. To effectively utilize the generated data, we also developed a novel cross-ensemble transfer technique, where the model is trained on a composite dataset in a semi-supervised manner and then fine-tuned on a small set of labeled data. This technique enhances the model's accuracy by adapting it to real-world conditions. We evaluated our method on the datasets "Tamil Handwritten Documents" from the IFG collection and "Bangla Handwritten Text" from the ICYTS collection, showcasing significant improvement in model performance with our single-shot data augmentation and cross-ensemble transfer techniques. The source code and datasets can be accessed via the following link: https://github.com/VidyuSH/SiSDA_CET_HTR. This research was partially funded by UGC Jammu. 

Keywords: Handwritten Text Recognition, Single-shot data augmentation, Semi-supervised learning, Convolutional Auto-Encoders, Cross-ensemble transfer, Low resource scenarios.

Recent merges of different methodologies have revitalized the field of ab initio nuclear physics, combining the strengths of various techniques to compute nuclear properties directly from the underlying quantum mechanics. This concept is systematically merged for the first time with the low-energy conditional inhibition technique to calculate accurately the long-range behavior of nuclear two-body interactions, thereby circumventing the limitations of conventional models. A novel approach is developed to model the high-momentum components of three-body interactions in a direct and model-independent manner, utilizing the properties of QCD. By incorporating these interactions into ab initio framework calculations, the ground-state properties of several isotopes, including Deuterium, Tritium, and 6 Li, are computed precisely. Furthermore, the merged interactions are found to describe the data on the d-T scattering length with exceptional accuracy, demonstrating a 5 times improvement over previous results. These merged interactions are expected to facilitate highly accurate ab initio computations of heavier nuclei and play a crucial role in understanding nuclear physics in the quark-gluon scale of QCD. Additionally, the merged interactions open up new avenues for experimental nuclear physics, enabling the prediction and identification of novel isomers through the calculated low-energy excitation spectra of heavier nuclei. The proposed methodology sets the groundwork for merged computations of the nuclear phase shifts, enabling the direct calculation of the nucleon-nucleon radiative correlation function and potentially shedding light on the quark interactions in the very low momentum region of QCD. The merged interactions also make it feasible to compute the Dirac and isospin-symmetry broken nuclear form factors, thereby enabling the calculation of the nuclear radii, their variations with mass, and the quark-like isospin-symmetry breaking in the nuclear phase shifts. The novel 6 Li isospin-symmetry breaking pattern is found to be strikingly analogous to the quark-gluon interaction predicted by QCD at very low momentum. The merged interactions thus provide a direct link between the quark-gluon and nucleon-nucleon interactions, thereby validating the QCD-inspired four-body interaction model, the Quark-Meson Coupling model. The merged interactions are anticipated to greatly deepen our understanding of the complex nuclear many-body problem and the quark-gluon interactions, thereby facilitating further research into the non-perturbative properties of QCD at very low momentum. The extra layer of information provided by geometry enables novel phenomena, as evident in topological quantum systems where specific properties persist despite changes in size or shape.  The steady flow of new materials has furthered understanding, but designing a system's topology in a predictable, controllable manner remains an open question. The rise of object-based programming on GPUs has been hindered by the limitations of memory allocation, leading to suboptimal performance due to underutilized device memory and fragmentation. Current solutions fail to address memory allocation's high concurrency requirements on GPUs, resulting in significant runtime overhead. To overcome these challenges, we present DynaSOAr, a highly efficient memory allocator designed for object-based programming on GPUs, with a flexible design suitable for a variety of use cases. DynaSOAr boasts several innovative features, including an optimized memory allocation scheme with minimal overhead, the ability to efficiently handle memory deallocation, and a dynamic memory allocation system that adapts to program requirements and optimizes GPU memory usage. Furthermore, DynaSOAr incorporates a superblock-based memory allocation scheme to reduce fragmentation and improves memory access by introducing a cache-aware page size. Our experimental results show that DynaSOAr outperforms state-of-the-art allocators by up to 2.3 times, with a significant reduction in memory allocation overhead of up to 20.1 times. Measurements of a pressurized straw conduit made from Inconel 625 are presented, along with the associated analytical predictions. The conduit, which has an outer diameter of 0.1024 meters, was subjected to various internal pressures ranging from 0 to 100 kPa. The findings indicate that the conduit's wall thickness varies by approximately 0.0625 millimeters along its length, which is necessary to maintain structural stability. The experimental data show acceptable correspondence with theoretical predictions using a general, three-dimensional elasticity model. The effects of radial and axial strain on the conduit's material properties and their influence on the conduit's overall shape are also examined. The findings suggest that both strain types have a significant impact, up to a few percent, on the conduit's overall shape, particularly near the closed end. The measurements confirm that the conduit's wall thickness gradation is necessary to prevent the onset of buckling under external pressure. The presence of a few millimeter-sized wrinkles on the conduit's surface, which are also captured by the analytical model, is also documented. The findings of these experiments can be applied to the design of long, thin, pressure-containing vessels, such as particle detectors and other scientific instruments. The measurements also highlight the significance of considering a conduit's three-dimensional structure in both its fabrication and operational contexts. The rotation measure of gas within the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) in the Milky Way can be determined by examining how gas mass is arranged in this ring-like structure.  We consider two scenarios based on the galactic bar's influence on the CMZ's geometry: one with a perfect circle and the other with an ellipse aligned with the galactic plane.  By calculating the angular rotation of the ellipse within the plane, we can represent the ellipses using Cartesian coordinates, $a$ and $b$, which facilitate the analysis through a 2D correlation function.  This method enables us to identify the most massive location of the CMZ and to estimate its mass by calculating the correlation peak.  As assumed mass distribution prototypes, we use three models with varying masses: a perfect circle and two elliptical shapes with different orientation angles.  We find that the rotating mass distribution in the CMZ is more complex than a simple circle, with the mass in the north-east exhibiting approximately ten percent more massive than in the south-west.  The estimated mass of the CMZ is approximately $9.1\times10^5$ solar masses, with further studies needed to validate the results and determine the mass spectrum of the forming star clusters.  This new method could be applied to other star-forming regions to help clarify their mass arrangement and rotation measures.  We propose three candidate regions for further study: M20, NGC 2076, and NGC 6720.  Additionally, we have developed a tool in Python that can reproduce our results, with the code available at https://github.com/astramoon/CMZ_tool.git.  This study provides the first quantitative assessment of the anisotropic mass distribution in the CMZ, a distinctive feature of our galaxy that is shaped by various physical processes.  By advancing our understanding of the CMZ's structure, we can improve our knowledge of its galactic bar and the rotation of its molecular gas clouds.  Further research is needed to verify our findings, determine the mass distribution in other star-forming regions, and clarify the galactic bar's influence on the CMZ's rotation.  This research has implications for studying the bar's shape and its effect on the CMZ's formation, as well as the galactic bar's impact on the CMZ's rotation.  This research paves the way for further exploration of the galactic bar's influence on the CMZ and the rotation of its gas clouds. We present a distorted resolvent method to construct Nash equilibria in differential games. The approach relies on an exact distorsion of the original Nash equilibrium equation, allowing for a Liapunov function to be established and subsequent convergence analysis. We provide multiple examples and outcomes to demonstrate the method's efficacy and versatility. 

On one hand, we show that any Nash equilibrium can be obtained through distorsion, thus illustrating various distorsion mechanisms that can yield exact equilibria. Conversely, we examine the limitations of the method by identifying cases where distorsion may fail to produce exact equilibria, albeit distorsion itself being possible.

In our first series of examples, we focus on a linear quadratic differential game, obtaining a Nash equilibrium via distorsion and subsequently proving its global stability. Building on this concept, we develop a category of distorsion mechanisms called "regular distorsion," which facilitates the construction of Nash equilibria in a broader class of games. We then propose an algorithm grounded in the regular distorsion method and, through theoretical analysis, establish its convergence and optimal values under certain conditions.

In our second series of examples, we explore a model of economic adjustment dynamics, obtaining a Nash equilibrium via distorsion and proving its global stability. We then extend the approach to distorsion-based equilibrium construction in finite-dimensional games, proposing an algorithm grounded in the regular distorsion method and demonstrating its convergence and optimal values under certain conditions.

Ultimately, we discuss the potential applications and extensions of the distorted resolvent method, encompassing various distorsion mechanisms such as time-scale distorsion, model predictive control, and the maximum entropy method. We envision the methodology to contribute significantly to the study of nonlinear differential games and optimal control. Additionally, the method is expected to be adaptable in various fields, including physics and engineering, through translation from mathematical concepts to real-world problems. Conversely, the methodology may also facilitate the reversal of this translation process, enabling a more intrinsic understanding of the underlying systems and their interactions. 

\textit{Note: The presented work is a revised version of the authors' initial study, which can be found in arXiv:2008.01939, with significant expansions and improvements.}

The application of this theory is challenging when dealing with non-equilibrium transformations, especially in situations where the Hamiltonian's potential energy component changes significantly. This dilemma is addressed by dividing the phase space into separate layers, each corresponding to a specific free energy level, and applying Nose-Hoover dynamics to simulate the collective behavior of these layers. This method is successfully applied to determine the thermally induced breakdown of a 2D Lennard-Jones crystal and the statistical mechanics-based estimation of the kinetic barrier for crystal-to-glass transitions in binary Lennard-Jones mixtures. Furthermore, this approach facilitates an efficient exploration of configuration space to identify the lowest energy structures of a system, as in the case of the propanone molecule's conformation space. This method can be extended to simulate unconstrained expansions of fluids, where the application of canonical ensemble statistics enables the achievement of thermodynamic equilibrium. This concept is demonstrated through an experiment involving a Lennard-Jones fluid in a narrow tube. This innovative method, which we refer to as the "Nose-Hoover layer method," has numerous potential applications in analyzing a wide array of complex phenomena, including the formation and transformation of nanomaterials, biomolecular folding, and surface patterning. Recently, attention-based transformer models have gained popularity in computer vision, delivering impressive results. Unlike conventional neural networks, which follow feed-forward processing, transformer models rely on sequential attention mechanisms, leading to improved representation quality. However, they require significantly more data for training, typically in the form of large-scale self-supervised learning tasks. In this study, we investigate the adoption of transformer architecture for self-supervised learning, leveraging its inherent benefits. Our experiments demonstrate the importance of using a parameter-efficient autoencoder design, incorporating the Swin Transformer's patch-based structure, for obtaining desirable traits. The proposed framework, dubbed "Traformer," sets a new benchmark in performance for multiple self-supervised learning evaluation metrics. Our findings also highlight the distinct advantages of trajectory learning methods. A comprehensive analysis of the characteristics of transformer-based representations is also provided. The code and model weights are publicly available for reproduction of our results. Additionally, our findings inspire the design of a novel transformer-based downstream encoder, enhancing the overall efficiency of self-supervised learning methods. Our approach outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods by a substantial margin on multiple datasets, as validated through rigorous evaluation on linear probing, k-NN, and end-to-end training protocols. Specifically, our method exhibits a notable improvement of 4-5% in accuracy compared to Swin-Transformers, trained end-to-end on ImageNet using a conventional loss function, for linear probing on ImageNet. A comparable level of performance gains were observed on other datasets, further solidifying the merits of our design choices. The associated model hyperparameters are documented, demonstrating the general applicability of our approach to diverse datasets, including ImageNet, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, as well as its compatibility with teacher-student training protocols. Moreover, our method outperforms prior work not only on well-documented datasets but also on self-supervised learning benchmarks, including the previously challenging NP-Discriminative Patch Discriminative (NPDPD) benchmark. Our approach represents a groundbreaking advancement in self-supervised learning, primarily due to the novel transformer-based encoder design, which generates distinctive, data-driven representations. These representations exhibit a notable shift in distribution compared to those obtained from conventional neural networks, as demonstrated through multiple evaluation metrics and analyses. Our method facilitates downstream task performance without the need for expensive labeled data, relying solely on self-supervised learning. As a result, trajectory learning-based self-supervised learning methods have reached new heights of performance, surpassing prior state-of-the-art methods by a substantial margin

In contrast, high-energy motions, typically fast and complex, pose greater challenges for analyzing human movement patterns.
By applying machine learning to categorize both low and high-energy motions, researchers can develop new insights into human dynamics.

Predicting climate change has significant practical value, yet accurate long-term forecasting remains a difficult task due to the inherent complexity and unpredictability of climate systems. The primary challenge lies in the non-local, long-distance spatiotemporal interactions within these systems, which demand a model with strong non-linearity and ability to capture distant connections. The application of neural networks in climate forecasting has shown promise, with models like CNN-LSTM and CNN-RNN models demonstrating efficacy in various forecasting tasks. More recently, long-distance information models such as CNN-VAE, CNN-AE, and Self-Attention model have been successfully used in climate forecasting. However, these models often prioritize local details over accuracy in predicting large-scale patterns. In response, we introduce the Transformer network with a shifted window of cross-attention, which captures non-local features and focuses on large-scale patterns to enhance accuracy in climate forecasting. The proposed model is evaluated using real NOAA data for monthly sea-ice forecasting and shows improved results compared to state-of-the-art models, with a significant enhancement of 2-4% in RMSAE values. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/ArashAradini/CLiMF.git. The model's performance in predicting large-scale patterns has been confirmed through comprehensive visual evaluations and statistical tests, showcasing its ability to predict the disappearance of sea ice 12 months in advance with high precision. The model's ability to capture distant connections is demonstrated through the visualization of its attention maps, which reveal the model's focus on critical features like El Ni\^no and El Ni\^no-Lan conditions. The proposed model exhibits exceptional generalization, displaying improved results compared to baseline models even when trained on a smaller dataset and tested on an unseen set of testing data. The model's efficiency is notable, with a processing time of 0.0003 seconds for a 12-month prediction, significantly faster than existing models. The model's accuracy in predicting climate patterns extends beyond simple forecasting, with a 10% improvement in predicting the onset of El Ni\^no conditions and a 5.5% improvement in predicting the state of Northern Greenland sea ice. The model's ability to predict climate changes has significant practical value and extends beyond simple forecasting, making it an invaluable tool for climate prediction and research. A parametrized family of Tversky metrics is introduced, and its connection to Tversky's original choice of parameterization is established.  The choice of the parameterization $s=1$ (known as the Jaccard distance), as well as seven other values of $s$, is analyzed.  The properties of the metric's indifference factor are investigated, and a method for effectively estimating its value from data is developed.  The metric's connection to a variation of the normalized information distance is studied, and specific values of $s$ are identified that result in the metric's equality to this variation under specific conditions.  The theorem demonstrating the relationship between the metric's score and the size of overlapping sets, given a particular $s$, is proven.  The diversity increase factor, a new concept, is introduced and its relationship to $s$ and the metric's indifference factor is investigated.  The metric's application to the analysis of a social network is a potential area of exploration.  The metric's score, or similarity score, is a real number between 0 and 1 that quantifies the similarity between two sets.  It can be viewed as a generalization of the Jaccard distance, and is defined as the ratio of the sizes of the overlapping sets $A$ and $B$ to the size of $A$, or vice versa.  The metric's indifference factor, or weighting factor, is a nonnegative real number that controls how the sizes of the sets $A$ and $B$ contribute to the metric's score.  The metric's diversity increase factor, or homogeneity factor, is a nonnegative real number that controls how the sizes of the sets $A$ and $B$ change when an element is added or removed from one of the sets. Recent advancements in motion deblurring have shown promising results, with clear patterns emerging from both theoretical and practical analyses. The development of advanced neural networks, such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), has significantly contributed to these breakthroughs. Inspired by self-supervised pre-training in language models, we propose the concept of Pseudo-Training, a novel approach that leverages internal data to enhance model performance. Specifically, we utilize a pre-trained model to generate blurs from a central frame, then apply it to real blurs through minimization. This strategy enables the model to tap into the inherent characteristics of its target distribution, mimicking the effect of large-scale labeled datasets. The integration of Pseudo-Training has yielded state-of-the-art deblurring performance on diverse datasets, encompassing images of humans, trees, and static scenes. The effectiveness of this technique stems from its ability to amplify the model's exposure to its target distribution, thereby boosting performance. The proposed method is also adaptable to various fields, offering a universal solution for addressing data insufficiency. The source code for this approach is publicly available.

This 'tunable neuron' can be adjusted to achieve either gradual or sudden changes in output, depending on the desired response shape. We developed two main components: a DNA stem structure that provides the base and oligonucleotide tails responsible for binding to form the DNA complex. By modifying the lengths of these tails, we varied the binding kinetics of the complex, thereby tuning the neuron's behavior. Additionally, we incorporated a DNA Aptamer that acts as a sensor, binding to specific oligonucleotides to mimic a neuron's response to distinct inputs. This design allows for rapid output changes, while also providing a stable and persistent output signal. Our research demonstrates the potential for accurately tuning DNA complex response times using a straightforward and controllable method. This construct has the potential to be integrated into fully functional spiking neural networks for addressing complex problems. Furthermore, the modular design can be adapted for a range of applications beyond neural networks, such as developing artificial cognitive systems and advanced sensors. This study presents the first instance of a fully functional, programmable spiking neuron built using DNA technology, paving the way for the widespread use of DNA-based constructs in biological computing systems. These DNA-based neural networks could even be implemented in living cells as a biologically natural computation method with the potential for self-updating networks.
