A strengthened form of this theory, proposed by Komlos, Plesnik, Tuza, and Simonovits in 1986, suggests that a graph with a chromatic number of $t$ and a large enough size will inevitably contain a complete subgraph of size $t$. In the present work, we provide evidence supporting this modified Hadwiger Theory for graphs with 4 and 5 colors, but not necessarily those that are dense. In contrast to earlier proofs, our work relies on the concept of pseudominors rather than the removal lemma. A novel aspect of our proof includes the application of a random Gales-Thomas model, first introduced by Gales and Thomas in 1980, as a tool for creating the required pseudominors. At the core of this model lies a random ordering of the vertices, derived from a Galton-Watson tree, in which the root is assigned a color at random. Furthermore, for every vertex in this tree, its parent is assigned a color at random, provided that the chosen color does not conflict with the previously assigned color. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the complete subgraph arising from this model should be considered a 'legitimate' complete subgraph. Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) are a group of machine learning models that process complex data in the form of graph structures. They combine graph filters with convolutional neural networks to achieve impressive results in graph-related applications. However, the theoretical underpinnings of GCNNs are still not fully understood. In this study, we develop a novel framework to elucidate the foundational principles of GCNNs using a new approach based on matched filtering. This method not only provides a general theoretical foundation for GCNNs but also offers an efficient and effective implementation of the models. Our findings, supported by numerical experiments, demonstrate that the matched filtering method can produce equivalent outcomes to existing GCNNs while offering improved performance and reduced computational requirements. Additionally, our method can adapt to various problem settings by modifying the matched filters. The resulting models exhibit improved accuracy and efficient computational complexity. Furthermore, our study quantitatively examines the effects of distinct nodes in the graph topology on the final output, revealing that nodes with long effective support (large k-hop connectivity) contribute more significantly to the output than those with short effective support. Our proposed method also facilitates the exploration of nodes with unknown or extensive connectivity in the output, demonstrating the potential to reveal novel insights in graph-related applications. Thorough numerical evaluations confirm that our method outperforms or competes effectively with existing GCNN models in multiple scenarios. Furthermore, our method shows great potential for extension to related models, such as graph Recurrent Neural Networks, and we anticipate similar improvements in those models. The universal algebra of branes in string theory corresponds to the Borel subalgebra of a quantum group. To capture both reversible and irreversible transformations, we introduce the quantum Branes algebra, an extension of the Borel subalgebra, incorporating factors that account for time and temperature dependencies. Utilizing the principle of duality in conformal field theories, we generate the relevant branching rules, which enable a systematic approach to identifying braanes. This algebraic framework is then applied to study defect lines and their interactions within two-dimensional conformal field theories. Furthermore, we provide evidence that the branes algebra is a quotient of the colored rational part of the principal specialization of the Alexander and HOMFLY-PT polynomials. To validate these claims, we present a geometric interpretation of the branes algebra through a local model that incorporates time and temperature dependencies, specifically adapted from a study of Markov matrices. As a result, the relevance of time and temperature factors is intrinsic to the branes algebra, allowing for the generalization of Reversibility Principle to branes in string theory. This theory is implied by a geometric model that incorporates time and temperature factors, which we propose as a new structure for braanes in string theory. To demonstrate these claims, we first establish the relevance of time and temperature factors to braanes in string theory, which is confirmed through an analysis of the Gopakumar-Vafa invariants. These claims are also validated in tests for random branes and vanishing branes cases. Additionally, we found that the branes algebra is related to a subalgebra of the Ducek algebra, which is a quantization of the Novikov prime series. Finally, we found that braanes in string theory are related to Gopakumar-Vafa invariants through a duality principle, which is confirmed through an analysis of random branes and vanishing branes cases. These relationships between braanes, duality principles, and the Reversibility Principle are fundamental properties of string theory, as predicted by a geometric model that incorporates time and temperature dependencies. These claims are confirmed through a re-examination of the known results on braanes, which demonstrate how the Reversibility Principle can be generalized to braanes in string theory. Circular and nontransitive likelihoods present distinctive characteristics in terms of ranking data. While regular statistical models generally adhere to transitivity, accounting for unobserved data and incorporating prior information can yield unanticipated rankings. This paper investigates the properties of circular and nontransitive likelihoods, revealing that their minimization and maximization lead to inconsistent results, notably including the "preference paradox" in ranking data. To resolve these issues, this paper develops a novel framework for consistent estimation based on the skew-normal distribution, thereby facilitating reliable inference and efficient estimation. Additionally, the paper examines how to generate rank-preferred prior distributions on the parameter space and discusses their practical implications. Lastly, the paper showcases a range of real-world applications where this framework excels in providing accurate inferences. Our theoretical analysis and empirical findings are substantiated through extensive numerical simulations. Most machine learning applications begin with a data science pipeline, which involves a labor-intensive process called model selection.  Model selection involves numerous options, with each choice being significant, although often underestimated.  Each model choice in the pipeline affects not only the accuracy but also the computational resources required, making some choices preferable in certain situations and not in others.  A comprehensive search through all possible models is often impractical, given the time-consuming and computationally expensive nature of some options.  In this paper, we investigate the potential of reducing the complexity of model selection through data-driven approaches, by asking if the optimal model choices can be predicted based on past training data, thus streamlining the specialisation process.  Our study explores this hypothesis through code specialization, a technique that involves the automatic modification of software code to match specific training data characteristics, in order to improve the accuracy of the models without extending the training time.  By drawing on recent breakthroughs in this area, we test various specialisation strategies on a range of regression algorithms and evaluate their effectiveness using metrics such as mean absolute error and the number of training iterations required.  Our experimental results show that the optimal model configurations can indeed be predicted and leveraged to accelerate the training process, with significant improvements in efficiency.  In particular, we find that the best practices learned from past training data can be applied to newly supplied data, thus enabling the development of highly specialised models without extending the training time.  Our code specialised models achieve up to 3.48 times faster training times, at the cost of a negligible reduction in accuracy.  In other words, the optimal model choices can be distilled from large datasets of different configurations, in order to accelerate the training process for more complex datasets.  This capability is illustrated through an example in which a specialisation strategy developed for a small dataset is applied to a range of related datasets, with consistent improvements in efficiency and accuracy.  Our findings validate the potential of data-driven approaches to reduce the complexity of model selection through specialisation, thus accelerating the training process for a range of regression algorithms.  In particular, we find that specialisation can be applied successfully to improve the efficiency and accuracy of models for solving inverse problems, by leveraging past training data to predict the most effective model configurations.  This research opens up new possibilities for the automatic development of specialized software code, tailored to the particular characteristics of the data on which it is trained, in order to accelerate the training process and improve the accuracy of the models. This "anti-Jaynes-Cummings" model undergoes Rabi oscillations more quickly with stronger coupling, but this increase accelerates beyond a point where the oscillations eventually collapse. The Active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck theory, a simplified model for self-propelled particles, generates diverse collective behavior when varying the persistence time and self-propulsion force. By adjusting these parameters, the system can be in either a stationary or mobile state. We found that during motion, the average speed of the particles and the speed at which the group's center moves differ significantly. Furthermore, the distance traveled by each particle is significantly greater than the displacement of the group's center, reflecting the variability in individual particle travel distances. Moreover, the distribution of individual particle travel distances is skewed, with the distance traveled by the group's center being normally distributed. These findings, confirmed through numerical and analytical examinations, demonstrate the substantial disparity in individual and group movements. Additionally, we analyzed the travel paths of the particles and the group and found their geometrical characteristics to be comparable, albeit the particle trajectories being more complex and irregular. The particle trajectories, observed under a microscope, resemble polymers' random walk paths, whereas the group's movement appears more organized and linear, resulting in a Roessler attractor when their directions are plotted on a two-dimensional plane. The emergence of this attractor is attributed to the collective motion's symmetry, broken by the individual particles' movements, leading to acausality where past events influence present movements. In other words, the current state of the system depends on its previous states, not solely on its immediate proximity in space or time. The occurrence of this attractor is a consequence of the system's nonlinear properties, evident in the long memory of the group's motion. This long memory is responsible for the non-Markovian behavior of the system, making it possible to analyze the past without requiring a detailed understanding of the present to predict the future. The system's non-Markovian characteristics are a direct result of the individual particles' movements, leading to a significant and extensive correlation in the distance traveled by adjacent particles. This extensive correlation is highly significant as it surpasses the system's dimensions, facilitating the system's transition from a homogeneous to a heterogeneous state. The individual particles' movements result in this long memory by establishing an intricate network of interconnected distances, extending far beyond the system's boundaries. This long memory enables the system to retain a permanent record of its past, making its evolution dependent on a lengthy timeline rather than a limited spatial range. The long memory of the system is a consequence of the Labor variations, a term that describes the difference in individual particle travel distances, demonstrating how the system's past influences its current state.

To facilitate language understanding without the need for extensive training data, researchers often employ cross-lingual transfer. This study focuses on transferring knowledge across languages in a classification task, and finds that existing techniques rely heavily on being able to translate class names between languages, which is not the case in this study as it uses a zero-shot approach. A new neural architecture, Task Depiction, is proposed to enable this transfer by generating a semantic representation of the classes for each task, allowing for cross-language understanding. Unlike previous approaches, Task Depiction does not rely on being able to translate class names and can handle languages without a standard script, as long as there is a shared knowledge space. It can also handle non-standard class labels by being trained on data that includes additional context. The effectiveness of Task Depiction is demonstrated through experiments on a range of languages and datasets, and it is found to perform better than existing transfer methods. It is also found to be more effective when there is limited data available for a new task, and when classes overlap with those in a trained model. A follow-up study shows that Task Depiction can be used to generate class descriptions in languages that do not use an alphabet, by using a shared space with an alphabet-based language. Task Depiction is found to perform better than a model that directly translates classes, and better than a model that uses a two-stage approach to classify in a non-native language. It is also found to perform better than a model that uses a different neural architecture, called Cross-Lingual-Space. The results show that Task Depiction can be used to enable cross-lingual transfer with a high degree of accuracy, and can be used to perform a range of natural language tasks in multiple languages. It is found to be particularly effective when there is limited data available for a new task, and when classes overlap with those in a trained model. A demonstration shows that Task Depiction can be used to enable cross-lingual transfer in a real-world application, and that it performs better than a model that directly translates classes. The code for Task Depiction is made available.

Ultimately, we find that these two approaches result in identical work outputs. A distinct topological insulating phase in Majorana systems can be stabilized through the combination of a Zeeman field and gate voltage. We developed a novel approach to deriving a universal style from a set of images, which is used to enhance their appearance with adjustable intensity. Our style extraction method identifies specific features in a set of images and represents them in a lower-dimensional space, capturing unique characteristics that define the desired style. This representation is applied to individual images through a generalized process, resulting in a reproduced set of images with similar stylistic features. To achieve more accurate results, we introduced a bidirectional algorithm that learns to map images from a neutral state to the desired style and vice versa. We demonstrated the effectiveness of our method on the task of global tone mapping, which adjusts image brightness to showcase scene details while preserving natural textures. Our method also enables global reverse tone mapping, which recovers images from the desired style, effectively removing excessive brightness. Our experiments show that the generated forward and reverse maps converge in the feature space, resulting in a reproducible and consistent style. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art models on the EPFL dataset and produces a converged map of images that retain original textures, as demonstrated in the generated demos. This report summarizes the outcomes of the 2022 CVPR competition focused on Air Quality Monitoring using Image Data (AQTC), specifically addressing the problem of identifying particulate matter (PM) in Chinese urban settings. The competition consisted of two challenges: a classification task and a segmentation task. The classification task required identifying PM in four different size ranges (coarse, medium, fine, and total), while the segmentation task involved pinpointing the center coordinates and bounding box of the coarse PM in images. The competition featured two stages, with data released in early March and winners announced in April 2022. A total of 61 teams participated in the classification challenge and 52 in the segmentation challenge. The top three teams in the classification challenge achieved remarkable results, with their top models showcasing high overall accuracy, with a particular team even reaching 95.86% accuracy on the private test set. Meanwhile, the top three teams in the segmentation challenge demonstrated excellent mean absolute errors (MAE) of 7.47, 7.35, and 7.34, with a particular team even reaching an MAE of 7.34 on the private test set. The winning teams employed diverse approaches, with some relying on data augmentation, transfer learning, and ensemble techniques. Specifically, the best model in the classification challenge utilized a pre-trained ResNet34 model with data augmentation techniques, ensemble techniques, and early stopping, achieving an overall accuracy of 95.86% on the private test set. Similarly, the best model in the segmentation challenge involved pre-trained ResNet34 with data augmentation and ensemble techniques, resulting in an MAE of 7.34 on the private test set. Notably, both winning models excelled in their respective challenges, with their top models showcasing exceptional results when evaluated on the private test set. The growing impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming various industries, however, the underlying algorithms that AI uses remain opaque to users, limiting understanding of its decision-making processes. A key challenge in implementing AI systems is developing a way to make its workings transparent to both developers and users. Explainable AI (XAI) promotes transparency by enhancing understanding of an AI model's decisions, which is crucial for building trust in AI-powered systems. Current XAI approaches primarily concentrate on technical aspects, but overlook the needs and perspectives of stakeholders. To address this gap, we suggest that Requirement Engineering (RE) can play a crucial role in developing a more user-centered approach to XAI. Specifically, we propose that requirements engineering can aid in creating a clear understanding of users' needs and the necessary explanations, thus driving the development of more transparent and understandable AI systems. This paper outlines our initial thoughts on how RE can contribute to the XAI field, drawing from prior research and exemplars. It aims to stimulate further discussion and exploration of the intersection between RE and XAI. Ultimately, this collaboration has the potential to foster a more transparent and trustworthy AI environment. Keywords: Explainable AI, Artificial Intelligence, Requirements Engineering, Transparency, Trust.

Reinforcement learning typically assumes a static environment, but most real-world scenarios involve dynamic settings where resources are allocated and time passes. Current RLS methods are designed for a specific horizon, and are often reset or taken to completion. We propose two new approaches, both of which train continuously in time. The first, Q-learning with time aggregation, adapts existing Q-learning by aggregating experiences over time and learning from cumulative rewards. In contrast, the second, called time-transformed Q-learning, employs a transformation of the state-action value function that naturally incorporates temporal considerations, thus eliminating the need for time aggregation. We demonstrate that both methods allow for continuous training without resetting the episode, and can be optimized to achieve similar regret bounds as traditional RLS methods. Furthermore, the approaches exhibit notable performance in experimental evaluations. Ultimately, the choice of method depends on whether episodes are reinitialized after each training period, in which case time-transformed Q-learning is preferred due to lower computational complexity, or whether training periods overlap, in which case time-aggregation is recommended due to better performance in such scenarios. The proposed methods also offer a novel understanding of the conditions under which continuous reinforcement learning is possible. Interestingly, we also observe that the time-transformed Q-learning framework shares intriguing connections with the fundamental limits of efficient computation, as well as the long-standing P vs. NP problem. Specifically, we show that continuous reinforcement learning may be intractable if the time horizon is not adequately restricted. This result turns out to be particularly accurate in the context of the specific problem we study, but we also hypothesize that this intractability might extend to a broader class of reinforcement learning problems. The proposed methods are accompanied by comprehensive theoretical analysis and experimental validation, along with an open-source code repository for easy reproduction. The main results were formally presented at the 2022 ICML conference, and are further expanded upon in this manuscript. The related hypothesis on the intractability of continuous reinforcement learning will be formally presented at NeurIPS 2022.
